Phone hacking by news organizations became the subject of scandals that raised concerns about illegal acquisition of confidential information by news media organizations in the United Kingdom, the United States and Australia between 1995 and 2012. The scandal had been simmering since 2002 but broke wide open in July 2011 with the disclosure that a murdered teenage girl's mobile phone had been hacked by a newspaper looking for a story. The scandals involved multiple organizations, and include the [[News of the World royal phone hacking scandal|''News of the World'' royal phone hacking scandal]], the [[News International phone hacking scandal]], the [[2011 News Corporation scandals]], and the [[Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal]].

By 2002, the practice of [[Phone hacking scandal reference lists#Publications mentioned in the ICO Report|publications using private investigators]] to acquire confidential information was widespread in the United Kingdom,<ref name=WhatPricePrivacy/> with some individuals using illegal methods.<ref name=GuardianRees20020921aA>{{cite news|last=McLagan|first=Graeme|title=Fraudster squad- Graeme McLagan on the black economy run by corrupt police and private detectives|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2002/sep/21/privacy2|accessdate=28 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=21 September 2011}}</ref><ref name=GuardianRees20020921b>{{cite news|last=McLagan|first=Graeme|title=Journalists caught on tape in police bugging|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2002/sep/21/privacy|accessdate=29 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=21 September 2011}}</ref> Information was allegedly acquired by accessing private voicemail accounts, hacking into computers, making false statements to officials to obtain confidential information, entrapment,<ref name=NYTimesMcMullan201111>{{cite There was evidence that illegal acquisition of confidential information continued at least into 2010.<ref name=GuardianMcDonagh201209>{{cite news|last=O'Carroll|first=Lisa|title=Labour MP Siobhain McDonagh sues News International and the Sun|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2012/sep/10/siobhain-mcdonagh-labour-mp-news-international|date=10 September 2012|accessdate=10 September 2012}}</ref> Solicitors representing victims were targeted for surveillance by a news media organisation being sued as recently as 2011.<ref name=GuardianLewis20111107>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=News of the World hired investigators to spy on hacking victims' lawyers|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/nov/07/news-world-investigator-spy-lawyers|date=7 November 2011|accessdate=21 July 2012}}</ref> Illegal payments by news media agents to public officials continued into 2012.<ref>{{cite news|last=Plunkett|first=John|title=Met's corrupt payments probe widens to include Mirror and Star titles|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/jul/23/met-corrupt-payments-mirror-star|date=23 July 2012|accessdate=25 September 2012}}</ref>

==Early investigations (1990s–2005)==
During this period, illegal acquisition of confidential information for developing news stories was widespread.  News media journalists, editors and executives, along with private investigators, public officials, and police officers, all benefited from the practice.  Little was done to inhibit it.

===Victims===
{{Main|List of news media phone hacking scandal victims}}
In 2000, eight-year-old Sarah Payne was murdered by a paedophile. ''[[News of the World]]'' and its then editor, [[Rebekah Brooks]] (née Wade), championed the campaign led by Sarah's mother for legislation to notify parents if a child sex offender lived nearby.  Brooks gave Sarah's mother a mobile phone to facilitate communication.  The phone was subsequently hacked by an agent of ''[[News of the World]]''.<ref>{{cite news|author1=Davies, Nick  |author2=Amelia Hill |name-list-style=amp |title=News of the World targeted phone of Sarah Payne's mother|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/28/phone-hacking-sarah-payne|accessdate=21 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=28 July 2011}}</ref>

Six months later, [[Paul McCartney|Sir Paul McCartney]] left a voicemail message for his then girlfriend, [[Heather Mills]], trying to work things out.<ref>{{cite news|last=Greenslade|first=Roy|title=Piers Morgan and phone hacking – what his record really reveals|newspaper=The Guardian- Greenslade Blog|date=29 July 2011}}</ref>  [[Mirror Group]] journalists hacked the phone to listen in.<ref>{{cite news|last=Robinson|first=James|title=Heather Mills claims Mirror Group journalist admitted hacking her phone|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/aug/03/heather-mills-phone-hacking|date=3 August 2011|accessdate=2 August 2012}}</ref>  [[Piers Morgan]], editor of the ''[[Daily Mirror]]'' at the time, later acknowledged listening to it.<ref>{{cite news|last=Doward|first=Jamie|title=Piers Morgan under pressure as phone-hacking scandal widens| url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/aug/06/piers-morgan-phone-hacking-scandal |newspaper=The Guardian|date=6 August 2011|accessdate=26 April 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite AV media |people= |date= |title=Former Daily Mirror editor Piers Morgan: Heather Mills tape source |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G4Kg96y_4Pw |access-date= 26 April 2023 |publisher= YouTube}}</ref>

When teenager Milly Dowler disappeared in 2002, agents of ''[[News of the World]]'' hacked into her mobile phone messages hoping to acquire information they could use for a story.  [[Surrey Police|Surrey police]] were reportedly advised of this hacking at the time, but no action was taken.<ref>{{cite news|last=Laville|first=Sandra|title=Senior police officer under investigation over hacking of Milly Dowler's phone|newspaper=The Guardian}}</ref>

Journalists working at ''News of the World'' after [[Andy Coulson]] became chief editor in 2003 claimed that Coulson talked freely about using the "dark arts," including phone hacking,<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901>{{cite news|last1=Van Natta |first1=Don Jr. |author2=Jo Becker |author3=Grahm Bowley  |name-list-style=amp |title=Tabloid Hack Attack on Royals, and Beyond|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/05/magazine/05hacking-t.html|accessdate=17 September 2011|newspaper=The New York Times|date=1 September 2010}}</ref> and that "everybody knew. The office cat knew."<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/> There were thousands of phone hacking victims during this period from all walks of life.<ref name=GuardianMotorman20090830>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=Operation Motorman: the full story revealed|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2009/aug/31/press-privacy-information-commmissioner|accessdate=21 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=30 August 2009}}</ref> The [[Metropolitan Police Service]] and the [[Information Commissioner's Office|Information Commissioner's Office (ICO)]] accumulated huge amounts of evidence that confidential information was being obtained illegally for use by news organisations including [[News Corporation (1980–2013)|News Corporation]]'s subsidiary [[News International]] (''News of the World'', ''The Sun'', ''The Times''), [[Mirror Group Newspapers]] (''Daily Mirror''), [[Express Newspapers]] (''Daily Star'', ''Daily Express''), and others.  But almost a decade was to pass before dogged investigative reporting by ''[[The Guardian]]'' newspaper generated public outrage over the invasions of privacy that had been covered up through wilful blindness, intimidation, and suppression of evidence by news organisations, law enforcement organisations, and politicians.

During 2003 and 2004 in the United States, someone at [[News Corporation (1980–2013)|News Corporation]]'s advertising subsidiary, [[News America Marketing]], repeatedly hacked into a computer at rival FLOORgraphics to obtain confidential product and contract information with which to put FLOORgraphics at a disadvantage in a brutal competitive battle.  The FBI initiated an investigation, but little effort was put into it.<ref name=MSNBCFloorgraphics20110721>{{cite news|last=Isikoff|first=Michael|title=US looks into alleged hacking by News Corp.'s ad arm|url=http://today.msnbc.msn.com/id/43847056/ns/today-today_news/t/us-looks-alleged-hacking-news-corps-ad-arm/#.TlAyqju7P_0|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110724031025/http://today.msnbc.msn.com/id/43847056/ns/today-today_news/t/us-looks-alleged-hacking-news-corps-ad-arm/#.TlAyqju7P_0|url-status=dead|archive-date=24 July 2011|accessdate=20 August 2011|publisher=MSNBC|date=21 July 2011}}</ref> In 2006 an editor of ''[[News of the World]]'' reportedly hacked into the computer of a British Army intelligence officer in Northern Ireland who had responsibility for contact with an agent embedded in the Provisional IRA and potentially at high risk for assassination if his whereabouts became known.<ref name=DaviesRees20110609/><ref>{{cite news|last=Underhill|first=William|title=Hacking Scandal's Brush With Terror|url=http://www.thedailybeast.com/articles/2011/08/03/news-international-twist-ian-hurst-computer-hacking-allegations.html|accessdate=21 August 2011|newspaper=The Daily Beast|date=3 August 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.channel4.com/news/hacking-scandal-met-launches-new-probe|title=Hacking Scandal – Met Launches New Probe|publisher=Channel 4 News|date=29 July 2011|accessdate=21 August 2011}}</ref> Again, law enforcement officials did little to investigate the charges at the time.<ref>{{cite news|last=Harper|first=Tom|title=Met 'failed to act over hacking of ex-Army spy's IRA emails'|url=http://saoirse32.blogsome.com/2011/08/03/met-failed-to-act-over-hacking-of-ex-army-spys-ira-emails/|accessdate=21 August 2001|newspaper=SAOIRSE32|date=1 August 2011|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927094009/http://saoirse32.blogsome.com/2011/08/03/met-failed-to-act-over-hacking-of-ex-army-spys-ira-emails/|archivedate=27 September 2011|df=dmy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=An overlooked Panorama scoop as a British soldier breaks cover|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/greenslade/2011/mar/16/bbc-ireland|accessdate=21 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian- GreensladeBlog|date=16 March 2011}}</ref>

Before public outrage forced rigorous investigations, evidence that several thousand UK citizens including celebrities, Members of Parliament, murder victims, their relatives, or anyone else who happened to be nearby, had been victims of phone hacking remained for many years consigned unexamined by officers of the [[Metropolitan Police Service]] to storage in [[Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal#Investigations of the Metropolitan Police|garbage bags in the bowels of New Scotland Yard.]]

===Operation Nigeria===
Private investigators and their sources who were illegally providing confidential information to ''News of the World'' were also engaged in a variety of other illegal activities.  Between 1999 and 2003, [[News International phone hacking scandal reference lists#Convictions|several were convicted for crimes]] including drug theft and distribution, child pornography, planting evidence, corruption, and [[perverting the course of justice]]. [[Jonathan Rees]] and his partner Sid Fillery, a former police officer, were also under suspicion for the [[Daniel Morgan (private investigator)|ax murder of a third private investigator]].  The Met undertook [[Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal#Operation Nigeria (1999)|Operation Nigeria]] and tapped Rees' telephone.   A large quantity of evidence was accumulated that Rees was purchasing information from improper sources and that [[News International phone hacking scandal reference lists#Individuals who worked for both News International and the police|Alex Marunchak]] of ''[[News of the World]]'' was paying as much as £150,000 a year for it.<ref name=GuardianRees20110311/> The operation was discontinued and Rees arrested when he was heard planning to plant false evidence to assist a client.<ref name=GuardianRees20020921b/><ref name=GuardianRees20110311/> He was convicted in 2000 and sent to prison for five years. Fillery was convicted for child pornography in 2003.<ref name=GuardianRees20110608b>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jun/08/phone-hacking-scandal-jonathan-rees |title=Phone-hacking scandal: Jonathan Rees obtained information using dark arts |author=Davies, Nick |work=The Guardian |date=8 June 2011 |accessdate=14 August 2011 }}</ref><ref name=GuardianRees20110311>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=Jonathan Rees: private investigator who ran empire of tabloid corruption|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/mar/11/jonathan-rees-private-investigator-tabloid|accessdate=18 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=11 March 2011}}</ref>

Instead of distancing themselves from the suspected murderers, ''News of the World'' editors began, in June 2002, surveillance on one of the Met police officers investigating the murder. Intended or not, this had the potential for undermining the murder investigation of ''News of the World'' sources.  Fillery reportedly used his relationship with Alex Marunchak to arrange for private investigator [[Glenn Mulcaire]], then doing work for ''News of the World'', to obtain confidential information about Detective Chief Superintendent David Cook.  This included his home address, his internal payroll number at the Metropolitan police, his date of birth and figures for the amount that he and his wife were paying for their mortgage. Surveillance of Cook is also reported to have involved physically following him and his young children.  It included attempts to access his voicemail and that of his wife, and possibly attempts to send a "Trojan horse" email to try to steal information from his computer.  Documents reportedly in the possession of the Scotland Yard shows that "Mulcaire did this on the instructions of [[Greg Miskiw]], assistant editor at ''News of the World'' and a close friend of Marunchak."   It also appeared that attempts had been made to open letters that had been left in Cook's external postbox.<ref name=GuardianBrooks20110706>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=News of the World surveillance of detective: what Rebekah Brooks knew|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/06/news-of-the-world-rebekah-brooks|accessdate=18 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=6 July 2011}}</ref> The Metropolitan Police Service handled this apparent attempt by agents of ''[[News of the World]]'' to interfere with a murder inquiry of the newspapers private investigators by having informal discussions with [[Rebekah Brooks]], then editor for ''News of the World''. "Scotland Yard took no further action, apparently reflecting the desire of Dick Fedorcio, Director of Public Affairs and Internal Communication for the Met who had a close working relationship with Brooks, to avoid unnecessary friction with the newspaper."<ref name=GuardianBrooks20110706/>

No one was charged with illegal acquisition of confidential information as a result of Operation Nigeria, even though the Met reportedly collected hundreds of thousands of incriminating documents during the investigations into Jonathan Rees over his links with corrupt officers."<ref name=GuardianRees20110608a>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=Phone-hacking scandal widens to include Kate Middleton and Tony Blair|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2011/jun/08/phone-hacking-kate-middleton-tony-blair|accessdate=20 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=8 June 2011}}</ref><ref name="Dodd, Vikram and Sandra Laville">{{cite news|author1=Dodd, Vikram  |author2=Sandra Laville |name-list-style=amp |title=Scotland Yard in spotlight as axe murder case collapses|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2011/mar/11/scotland-yard-murder-case-daniel-morgan|accessdate=26 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=11 March 2011}}</ref> The Guardian's detailed expose of 2002<ref name=GuardianRees20020921b/> did not impel anyone at the Met or in public office to act.  Upon Rees' release from prison in 2005, he immediately resumed his private investigative work of profitably supplying confidential information to ''News of the World'', where [[Andy Coulson]] by that time had succeeded Rebekah Brooks as editor.

===Operation Motorman===
Many private investigators in addition to Rees were plying the lucrative trade in illegally acquired confidential information.<ref name=WhatPricePrivacy>{{cite web|title=What Price Privacy?|url=http://www.ico.gov.uk/~/media/documents/library/Corporate/Research_and_reports/WHAT_PRICE_PRIVACY.ashx|publisher=Information Commissioner's Office|date=10 May 2006|accessdate=20 August 2011|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110829133733/http://www.ico.gov.uk/~/media/documents/library/Corporate/Research_and_reports/WHAT_PRICE_PRIVACY.ashx|archivedate=29 August 2011|df=dmy-all}}</ref> John Boyall's speciality was acquiring information from confidential databases.  His assistant was [[Glenn Mulcaire]] until the autumn of 2001, when ''[[News of the World]]'s'' assistant editor, [[Greg Miskiw]], attracted Mulcaire away by giving him a full-time contract to do work for the newspaper.<ref name=GuardianRees20110311/> Boyall eventually attracted the attention of the [[Information Commissioner's Office|Information Commissioner's Office (ICO)]], an authority acting independently of the police in the public interest to uphold [[information privacy|data privacy]] rights for individuals.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ico.gov.uk/|title=Information Commissioner's Office|work=Information Commissioner's Office Website|publisher=Information Commissioner's Office|accessdate=23 September 2011|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120920050609/http://www.ico.gov.uk/|archivedate=20 September 2012|df=dmy-all}}</ref> The ICO raided Boyall's premises in November 2002.<ref name=WhatPricePrivacyNow>{{cite news|title=What Price Privacy Now?|url=http://www.ico.gov.uk/news/current_topics/what_price_privacy_now.aspx|accessdate=20 August 2011|newspaper=Information Commissioner's Office|date=December 2006|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110817034810/http://www.ico.gov.uk/news/current_topics/what_price_privacy_now.aspx|archivedate=17 August 2011|df=dmy-all}}</ref> Documents seized there led the ICO to raid the premises of yet another private investigator, Steve Whittamore under [[Operation Motorman (ICO investigation)|Operation Motorman]].<ref name="GuardianMotorman20090830"/> Documents from this raid included "more than 13,000 requests for confidential information from newspapers and magazines."<ref name=GuardianRees20110311/><ref name=GuardianCook20110706>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=News of the World surveillance of detective: what Rebekah Brooks knew|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/06/news-of-the-world-rebekah-brooks|accessdate=27 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=6 July 2011}}</ref> These established that confidential information was illegally acquired from telephone companies, the Driving & Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) and the [[Police National Computer]].  "Media, especially newspapers, insurance companies and local authorities chasing council tax arrears all appear in the sales ledger" of the agency.<ref name=WhatPricePrivacyNow/> Whittamore's network of information gatherers gave him access to confidential records at telephone companies, banks, post offices, hotels, theatres, and prisons, including [[BT Group]], [[Crédit Lyonnais]], [[Goldman Sachs]], [[Hang Seng Bank]], [[Glen Parva (HM Prison)|Glen Parva prison]], and [[Stocken (HM Prison)|Stocken prison]].<ref name=GuardianMotorman20090830/> Some 305 journalists working for [[News International phone hacking scandal reference lists#Publications mentioned in the ICO Report|at least 30 publications]] were found to be purchasing confidential information from private investigators.<ref name=ICO20061215>{{cite web|url=http://www.ico.gov.uk/news/current_topics/what_price_privacy_now.aspx|title=What Price Privacy Now?|publisher=Information Commissioners Office|date=15 December 2006|accessdate=18 July 2011|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110817034810/http://www.ico.gov.uk/news/current_topics/what_price_privacy_now.aspx|archivedate=17 August 2011|df=dmy-all}}</ref>

The ICO issued reports in May 2006 and December 2006 titled "What price privacy?" and "What price privacy now?"<ref name=ICO20061215/> However, much of the information obtained through Operation Motorman was not made public even after requests were made under the [[Freedom of Information Act 2000|Freedom of Information Act]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Background information from "What Price Privacy?" report|url=http://www.whatdotheyknow.com/request/background_information_from_what|work=What Do They Know.com- Make and explore Freedom of Information requests|publisher=What Do They Know.com|accessdate=10 October 2011|date=20 July 2011}}</ref> Although there was evidence of many people being engaged in illegal activity, relatively few were questioned.  Operation Motorman's lead investigator said during a 2006 inquiry that "his team were told not to interview journalists involved.  The investigator...accused authorities of being too 'frightened' to tackle journalists."<ref name=GuardianHenry20110914>{{cite news|last=Robinson, James and Ed Pilkington|title=Phone hacking: 7/7 disaster victim's mother to sue NoW publisher|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/sep/13/phone-hacking-disaster-victim-sues|accessdate=15 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=14 September 2011}}</ref>

===Operation Glade===
Learning that Whittamore was obtaining information from the police national computer, the Information Commissioner contacted the Metropolitan Police.  In response, the Met's anti-corruption unit initiated [[Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal#Operation Glade (2003)|Operation Glade]].<ref name=GuardianRees20110311/> Whittamore's detailed records identified 27 different journalists as commissioning his work, spending tens of thousands of pounds to acquire confidential information. Invoices submitted to [[News International]], owner of  ''News of the World,'' "sometimes made explicit reference to obtaining a target's details from their phone number or their vehicle registration."<ref name=GuardianMotorman20090830/> Between February 2004 and April 2005, the [[Crown Prosecution Service]] charged ten men working for private detective agencies with crimes relating to the illegal acquisition of confidential information.<ref name=GuardianGuilty20050416/><ref name=GuardianRees20110311/><ref name=GuardianPolicedata20050416>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2005/apr/16/pressandpublishing.crime |title=Police data sold to newspapers |author1=Cozens, Claire  |author2=Chris Tryhorn  |name-list-style=amp |work=The Guardian |date=16 April 2005 |accessdate=13 August 2011 }}</ref><ref name=PressGazetteGunning20050422>{{cite news|last=Watts|first=Mark|title=Private eyes charged with breaking data law in search of news scoops|url=http://www.pressgazette.co.uk/story.asp?storyCode=30261&sectioncode=1|accessdate=23 September 2011|newspaper=PressGazette|date=22 April 2005|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://archive.today/20130114020546/http://www.pressgazette.co.uk/story.asp?storyCode=30261&sectioncode=1|archivedate=14 January 2013|df=dmy-all}}</ref> No journalists were charged.<ref name="PressGazetteGunning20050422"/> Whittamore, Boyall, and two others pleaded guilty in April 2005. According to ICO head [[Richard Thomas (lawyer)|Richard Thomas]], "each pleaded guilty yet, despite the extent and the frequency of their admitted criminality, each was conditionally discharged [for two years], raising important questions for public policy."<ref name=GuardianRees20110311/><ref name=WhatPricePrivacyNow/>

==Royal household scandal (2005–2007)==
During this period the spectre of inappropriate, unpopular invasion of privacy became broadly publicised.  However, police officers, news media executives, the court took action that contained investigations and prevented the public from learning the true scope of the illegal activity.

===Discovery of phone hacking===
In November 2005, within months of the guilty pleas resulting from Operation Glade, the Metropolitan Police Service was notified of irregularities with the telephone voicemails of members of the royal household.  By January 2006, Scotland Yard determined there was an "unambiguous trail" to [[Clive Goodman]], the ''[[News of the World]]'' royal reporter, and to [[Glenn Mulcaire]], a private investigator who was contracted to do work for the paper."  The voicemail of one royal aide had been accessed 433 times.<ref name="NYTimesRoyals20100901"/>

The Met's counter-terrorism group, then led by assistant commissioner [[Andy Hayman]], had responsibility for the security of the royal family.  He was charged with making the investigation.<ref>{{cite news|title=Who's who in the Murdoch phone hacking scandal|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/whos-who-in-the-murdoch-phone-hacking-scandal/|access-date=10 October 2011|newspaper=CBS News- WorldWatch|date=19 July 2011}}</ref> There was concern about diverting resources to this effort because of the demands of other priorities, including following up on the 2005 London transit bombings and surveillance operations on possible bomb plotters.<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/>

On 8 August 2006, detectives from the Met went to ''[[News of the World]]'' with a [[search warrant]] to search Clive Goodman's desk.<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/> At the same time, police raided the home of Glenn Mulcaire and seized "11,000 pages of handwritten notes listing nearly 4,000 celebrities, politicians, sports stars, police officials and crime victims whose phones may have been hacked."<ref name=GuardianCorrupt20110707>{{cite news|author1=Laville, Sandra  |author2=Vikram Dodd |name-list-style=amp |title=Phone hacking: the hunt for corrupt officers and 4,000 possible victims|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/07/phone-hacking-hunt-officers-victims|accessdate=17 July 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=7 July 2011}}</ref><ref name=NYTimesScotlandYard20110716>{{cite news|last=Van Natta|first=Don Jr.|title=Stain From Tabloids Rubs Off on a Cozy Scotland Yard|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/07/17/world/europe/17police.html?_r=1&pagewanted=all|accessdate=17 September 2011|newspaper=The New York Times|date=16 July 2011}}</ref> The names included eight members of the royal family and their staff.<ref name=NYTimesScotlandYard20110716/> There were dozens of notebooks, two computers containing 2,978 complete or partial mobile phone numbers and 91 PIN codes, and 30 tape recordings made by Mulcaire.  Most significantly, there were at least three names of ''News of the World'' journalists in addition to Goodman, even though [[News International]] executives would later maintain Goodman was a single, "rogue reporter" involved in phone hacking.<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/> In the upper-left-hand corner of each document page was the name of the reporter or editor Mulcaire was helping.<ref name=NYTimesScotlandYard20110716/> Also seized was a recording of Mulcaire instructing a journalist how to hack into private voice mail, particularly easy if the phone's factory settings for privacy had not been changed.<ref name=NYTimesScotlandYard20110716/> All these documents went to Scotland Yard.

===Containment of the investigation===
[[File:Metropolitan Police Sign and Building in London.JPG|thumb|Investigations by the [[Metropolitan Police]] (Scotland Yard) in 2002 and 2006 were limited to just a few individuals, even though there was clear evidence of widespread phone hacking.<ref name=GuardianVerdicts20100224>{{cite news|last=Robinson|first=James|title=News of the World phone-hacking scandal: the verdicts|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2010/feb/24/phone-hacking-scandal-mps-verdicts|accessdate=20 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=24 February 2010}}</ref>]]

The seized documents also included a transcript of illegally accessed voice mail messages between Professional Football Association's [[Gordon Taylor (footballer)|Gordon Taylor]] and his legal adviser, Jo Anderson.  This document was titled [[News International phone hacking scandal reference lists#Key evidentiary documents|"Transcript for Neville"]] and is alleged to have been for [[Neville Thurlbeck]], another reporter for ''News of the World''.  This email demonstrated that use of illegal interception of voice mail messages was being used at ''[[News of the World]]'' by more than just Clive Goodman.  Met detectives did not then question Thurlbeck or any other ''News of the World'' journalist or any News International executives as part of their investigation.<ref name=GuardianNeville20110722>{{cite news|author1=Leigh, David  |author2=Nick Davies |name-list-style=amp |title=The 'For Neville' email: two words that could bring down an empire|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/22/for-neville-email-empire|accessdate=19 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=22 July 2011}}</ref><ref name=ParliamentYates20110902/><ref name="Leigh, David and Vikram Dodd">{{cite news|author1=Leigh, David  |author2=Vikram Dodd |name-list-style=amp |title=Key witness will testify on News of the World phone hacking|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2010/sep/07/news-of-the-world-phone-hacking-witness|accessdate=6 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=7 September 2010}}</ref> This failure to investigate may have been because of the Met's desire to maintain their comfortable relationship with the press.  According to ''The New York Times'':

{{Blockquote|Scotland Yard had a symbiotic relationship with ''[[News of the World]]''. The police sometimes built high-profile cases out of the paper's exclusives, and ''News of the World'' reciprocated with fawning stories of arrests.  Within days of the raids [on ''News of the World''], several senior detectives said they began feeling internal pressure. One senior investigator said he was approached by Chris Webb, from the police department's press office, who was 'waving his arms up in the air, saying, 'Wait a minute – let's talk about this' [and]...stressed the department's long-term relationship with [[News International]].<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/>}}

The Met's investigation under Hayman stayed narrowly focused on the victims in the royal household and a few other victims on a short "target list" seized by the Met during the Mulcaire raid.<ref name=NYTimesScotlandYard20110716/> Hayman had seen but had not acted upon a longer list that was 8 to 10 pages in length, single-spaced, that "read like a British society directory."<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/> Only the five other victims that were included in the indictment of Mulcaire were notified about violation of privacy. Of the thousands of people who may also have been victims, the Met decided to notify only those that were members of the government, police, military, or otherwise of national-security concern.  Not even all of these were notified. Politician [[George Galloway]] was notified by a detective on 24 August 2006 that his voicemail had been hacked and advised to change his PIN code to prevent re-occurrence. Galloway asked who had accessed his phone messages, but the detective refused to tell him.<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/>

Hayman's investigation also stayed narrowly focused on the activities of Goodman and Mulcaire.<ref name=NYTimesScotlandYard20110716/> No ''[[News of the World]]'' executives or reporters other than Goodman were questioned about phone hacking until [[Operation Weeting]] was initiated more than four years later.<ref name=GuardianWeatherup20110415>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/apr/14/phone-hacking-arrest-news-of-world |title=Unexpected arrest in phone-hacking case leaves News of the World stunned |author1=Hill, Amelia  |author2=Dan Sabbagh  |name-list-style=amp |work=The Guardian |date=15 April 2011 |accessdate=12 August 2011 }}</ref> Hayman enjoyed a comfortable relationship with the newspaper, having "attended four dinners, lunches and receptions with ''News of the World'' editors, including a dinner on April 25, 2006, while his officers were gathering evidence in the [Royal household phone hacking] case&nbsp;... Mr. Hayman left the Metropolitan Police in December 2007 and was soon [afterward] hired to write a column for ''[[The Times|The Times of London]]''", another publication owned and controlled by [[News International]].<ref name=NYTimesScotlandYard20110716/> These events later led to questions about whether Met officials having close relationships with news media organisations created inappropriate conflicts of interest.

Met officials consulted with the [[Crown Prosecution Service|Crown Prosecution Service (CPS)]], headed by [[Director of Public Prosecutions (England and Wales)|Director of Public Prosecutions]] (DPP) [[Ken Macdonald]], about the best general way to proceed with the investigation and prosecution.  The Met did not disclose all available evidence to senior CPS prosecutors at this time, reportedly omitting documents indicating that reporters in addition to Clive Goodman appeared to have been using Mulcaire's services.<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/> The CPS appears to have provided some rationale to the Met for limiting the investigation by initially advising that "phone hacking was only an offence if messages had been intercepted before they were listened to by the intended recipient."<ref name=GuardianMacdonald20110719>{{cite news|last=Bowcott|first=Owen|title=News Corp board shocked at evidence of payments to police, says former DPP|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/19/news-corp-police-payments-macdonald|accessdate=23 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=19 July 2011}}</ref> In fact, the hacking was illegal under the 1990 Computer Misuse Act regardless of whether messages had already been listened to by their intended recipient even if it was not illegal under the 2000 Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act. The precise nature of the guidance given by CPS to the Met became the subject of public disagreement between them 2011, at which time it was noted, among other things, that the charges brought against Goodman and Mulcaire included counts for which there was no mention or examination of whether messages had already been heard or not.<ref name=GuardianYates20110405>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=Phone-hacking case policeman John Yates under pressure to resign|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2011/apr/05/phone-hacking-john-yates-police|accessdate=10 October 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=5 April 2011}}</ref>

Goodman and Mulcaire were arrested in August 2006.<ref name=GuardianGoodman20110809>{{cite news|last=Jones|first=Sam|title=News of the World royal editor arrested over Clarence House phone tapping|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2006/aug/09/newsoftheworld.pressandpublishing|accessdate=12 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=9 August 2011}}</ref><ref name=IndependentBrooks20110922>{{cite news|author1=Cusick, James  |author2=Cahal Milmo |name-list-style=amp |title=Exclusive: Murdoch execs told of hacking evidence in 2006|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/crime/exclusive-murdoch-execs-told-of-hacking-evidence-in-2006-2358777.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220618/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/crime/exclusive-murdoch-execs-told-of-hacking-evidence-in-2006-2358777.html |archive-date=18 June 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|accessdate=10 October 2011|newspaper=The Independent|date=22 September 2011}}</ref> In November they both pleaded guilty to conspiracy to intercept communications without lawful authority with respect to three of the royal aides. They both were sent to prison.<ref>{{cite news| author =Tryhorn, Chris| title =Clive Goodman sentenced to four months| work =The Guardian| date =26 January 2007| url =https://www.theguardian.com/media/2007/jan/26/newsoftheworld.pressandpublishing1| accessdate =7 August 2011}}</ref> Mr. Goodman later claimed that he was promised he "could come back to a job at the newspaper if I did not implicate the paper or any of its staff in my mitigation plea."<ref name=GuardianGoodman20110816/><ref name=GuardianGoodmanLetter20110816>{{cite news|last=Robinson|first=James|title=Clive Goodman's letter to News International|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/interactive/2011/aug/16/clive-goodman-letter-phone-hacking|accessdate=16 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=16 August 2011}}</ref><ref name=GuardianEvidence20110816>{{cite news|last=Wapshott|first=Nicholas|title=Evidence of a News Corp coverup mounts|url=http://blogs.reuters.com/mediafile/2011/08/16/evidence-of-a-news-corp-coverup-mounts/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111026101009/http://blogs.reuters.com/mediafile/2011/08/16/evidence-of-a-news-corp-coverup-mounts/|url-status=dead|archive-date=26 October 2011|accessdate=16 August 2011|agency=Reuters MediaFile|date=16 August 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=News International letter 'was not redacted by police'|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/phone-hacking/8707918/News-International-letter-was-not-redacted-by-police.html|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120914132218/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/phone-hacking/8707918/News-International-letter-was-not-redacted-by-police.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=14 September 2012|accessdate=27 August 2011|newspaper=The Telegraph|date=17 August 2011}}</ref> He also later claimed that phone hacking was widely discussed at ''[[News of the World]]'' editorial meetings chaired by the editor, who at that time was [[Andy Coulson]].<ref name=GuardianMulcaire20110819/> In any event, after pleading guilty, being dismissed from ''News of the World'', and contesting that dismissal, Mr. Goodman was paid a full year's salary, worth over £90,000, £140,000 in additional compensation, and £13,000 to cover legal expenses. Tom Watson, member of the House of Commons committee looking into the illegal access of voicemail, concluded "It's hush money. I think they tried to buy his silence."<ref name="Davies">{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=Phone hacking: News of the World reporter's letter reveals cover-up|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/aug/16/phone-hacking-now-reporter-letter|accessdate=16 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=16 August 2011}}</ref> Mr. Mulcaire, following his guilty plea, received an £85,000 settlement<ref>{{cite web|title=Letter from John Turnbull to Committee, 15 August|url=http://www.parliament.uk/documents/commons-committees/culture-media-and-sport/PH23-John-Turnbull-to-Committee-15-Aug-2011.pdf|work=Letter from Linklaters to John Whittengale 15 August 2011|publisher=Linklaters|accessdate=26 August 2011}}</ref> and continued to receive financial support of £246,000 in legal fees from News International<ref name=HarneysMulcaire20110818>{{cite news|last=Harris|first=Joanne|title=News International's Mulcaire legal bill hit £250,000|url=http://www.thelawyer.com/news-internationals-mulcaire-legal-bill-hit-%C2%A3250000/1008962.article|accessdate=18 August 2011|newspaper=Harneys The Lawyer|date=18 August 2011}}</ref> until shortly after [[James Murdoch]] was publicly questioned about it during a House of Commons hearing.<ref>{{cite news|author1=Davies, Caroline  |author2=Lisa O'Carroll |name-list-style=amp  | title =Glenn Mulcaire legal payments terminated by News International| work =The Guardian| date =20 July 2011| url =https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/20/glenn-mulcaire-legal-fees | accessdate =7 August 2011}}</ref>

In short, the work of the Metropolitan police resulted in guilty pleas within 12-month of when the crimes against royal aides were committed.  However, it was abundantly clear from court testimony and documents in the possession of the Metropolitan Police that Mulcaire had hacked at least five other phones and that he completed work assignments for more than just Goodman at ''[[News of the world]]''.<ref name=GuardianGoodman20061120>{{cite news|last=Kiss|first=Jemima|title=Goodman pleads guilty|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2006/nov/29/newsoftheworld.pressandpublishing|accessdate=19 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=29 November 2006}}</ref><ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/> Mulcaire acknowledged hacking the phones of [[Sky Andrew]], [[Max Clifford]], [[Simon Hughes]], [[Elle Macpherson]], and [[Gordon Taylor (footballer)|Gordon Taylor]] in addition to members of the Royal household.<ref name=GuardianGoodman20061120/> These victims would all later bring suit against ''News of the World'' for invasion of privacy, some suits resulting in significant disclosures that would eventually lead to the collapse of the single "rogue reporter" stance maintained by News International.

Accordingly, within weeks of the arrests of Goodman and Mulcaire, a "senior police officer" reportedly advised [[Rebekah Brooks]] there was strong circumstantial evidence in the documents seized from Mulcaire that  ''[[News of the World]]'' journalists in addition to Goodman were implicated in phone hacking. In early autumn 2006, [[Tom Crone (barrister)|Tom Crone]], legal manager for [[News International]], reportedly contacted several other executives, including then ''[[News of the World]]'' editor [[Andy Coulson]], informing them of what the Met told Brooks.<ref name=IndependentBrooks20110922/> Coulson resigned, accepting responsibility for the illegal activity, but denied knowing about it.<ref name=GuardianRees20110311/> Nonetheless, senior newspaper executives including James Murdoch continued to maintain through early 2011 that the illegal activity was the sole work of this single "rogue reporter" and his private investigator.<ref>{{cite news|last=Somaiya|first=Ravi|title=British Parliament Will Question Former News Corp. Executive|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/10/12/world/europe/les-hinton-to-face-parliament-in-news-of-the-world-scandal.html?_r=1&hp|accessdate=11 October 2011|newspaper=The New York Times|date=11 October 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author1=Leigh, David  |author2=Nick Davies |name-list-style=amp | title =Phone hacking: Tom Crone and Colin Myler raise the stakes| work =The Guardian| date =22 July 2001| url =https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/21/tom-crone-colin-myler-analysis| accessdate =7 August 2011}}</ref>

The documents seized by the Met during the Mulcaire raid, including obvious evidence that many other people's phones had been hacked, remained largely unevaluated until the autumn of 2010.  No one at ''[[News of the World]]'' other than Goodman was questioned by the Met until March 2011.<ref name=GuardianWeatherup20110415/> Nonetheless, "senior Scotland Yard officials assured Parliament, judges, lawyers, potential hacking victims, the news media and the public that there was no evidence of widespread hacking by the tabloid."  ''The New York Times'' reported that "the police agency and News International … became so intertwined that they wound up sharing the goal of containing the investigation.<ref name="GuardianWeatherup20110415"/><ref>{{cite news| author =Natta, Don Van Jr.| title =Stain from Tabloids Rubs Off on a Cozy Scotland Yard | work =The New York Times| date =16 July 2011 | url =https://www.nytimes.com/2011/07/17/world/europe/17police.html?pagewanted=all| accessdate =7 August 2011}}</ref>

==Period of denials (2007–2010)==
During this period, evidence of phone hacking continued to come to the public's attention as a result of dogged investigative reporting, determined civil-suit plaintiffs, and related judicial rulings.  Efforts to make the public broadly aware of the scope of illegal acquisition of confidential information were frustrated by denials by news media organisations and police officials.

===Investigative reporting===
[[File:The Guardian Building Window in London.JPG|left|thumb|''[[The Guardian]]'' newspaper began early and remained at the forefront of reporting on the phone hacking scandal.]]

As early as 2002, when the [[Metropolitan Police Service|Metropolitan Police's]] anti-corruption unit was engaged in Operation Nigeria, ''[[The Guardian]]'' raised questions about whether all the evidence relating to police corruption was being pursued.<ref name="GuardianRees20020921aA" />

After the 2006 imprisonment of [[Clive Goodman]] and [[Glenn Mulcaire]], and with assurances from ''[[News International]]'' executives and senior [[Metropolitan Police]] officials that a thorough investigation of evidence had identified only these two as being involved in phone hacking, the public perception was that the matter was closed.  [[Nick Davies]] and other journalists from ''The Guardian'' continued to examine evidence available from court cases and reported information contradicting official positions.<ref name=GuardianRusbridger20110717/> Other newspapers ultimately followed suit, obtaining and evaluating information from court records, [[Freedom of Information Act 2000|Freedom of Information]] requests,<ref>{{cite news|title=Correspondence Between The New York Times and Scotland Yard|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2011/07/17/world/europe/20110717police-correspondence.html|accessdate=14 October 2011|newspaper=The New York Times|date=16 July 2011}}</ref> and field contacts, reportedly including police officers.

While [[Metropolitan Police Service|Scotland Yard]] and [[News International]] continued to insist that the practice of looking for news scoops by phone hacking was limited to a single "rogue reporter" and his private investigator, a small number of victims engaged solicitors and made civil claims for invasion of privacy.  As information about settlements on these suits leaked out, ''[[The Guardian]]'' newspaper reported about it, calling public attention to considerable evidence that the practice was widespread.  On 8 & 9 July 2009, the newspaper published three articles alleging that:

* [[Rupert Murdoch]]'s [[News Group Newspapers|News Group Newspapers (NGN)]] agreed to large settlements with hacking victims, including [[Gordon Taylor (footballer)|Gordon Taylor]].  The settlements included gagging provisions to prevent release to the public of evidence then held by the Metropolitan Police Service that NGN journalists repeatedly used criminal methods to get stories.  "News Group then persuaded the court to seal the file on Taylor's case to prevent all public access, even though it contained prima facie evidence of criminal activity."<ref name=GuardianGag20090708>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=Murdoch papers paid £1m to gag phone-hacking victims|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2009/jul/08/murdoch-papers-phone-hacking|accessdate=23 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=8 July 2009}}</ref> That evidence included documents seized in raids by the [[Information Commissioner's Office]] and by the Met between 2002 and 2006.<ref name=GuardianCoulson20090708>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=Trail of hacking and deceit under nose of Tory PR chief|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2009/jul/08/murdoch-newspapers-phone-hacking|accessdate=23 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=8 July 2011}}</ref>
* If the suppressed evidence became public, hundreds more phone hacking victims of [[News Group Newspapers]] (NGN), a subsidiary of [[News International]], might be in a position to take legal action against NGN newspapers including ''[[News of the World]]'' and ''[[The Sun (United Kingdom)|The Sun]]''.  It might also provoke police inquiries into reporters and senior newspaper executives.<ref name=GuardianGag20090708/>
* When [[Andy Coulson]], then chief press adviser to Prime Minister [[David Cameron]], was editor and deputy editor at ''[[News of the World]]'', journalists there openly engaged private investigators that used illegal phone hacking, paying invoices for this work that itemised illegal acts.<ref name=GuardianCoulson20090708/>
* Everybody at ''[[News of the World]]'' knew what was going on, that there was no public interest defence for the phone hacking, and that the way investigations had been pursued raised serious questions about the Metropolitan Police, the Crown Prosecution Service, and the court which, "faced with evidence of conspiracy and systemic illegal actions,...agreed to seal the evidence." rather than make it know to the public.<ref name=GuardianNeil20090708>{{cite news|last=Dodd|first=Vikram|title=Ex-Murdoch editor Andrew Neil: News of the World revelations one of most significant media stories of our time|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2009/jul/09/andrew-neil-murdoch-andy-coulson|accessdate=24 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=8 July 2009}}</ref>
* The Met held evidence that thousands of mobile phones had been hacked into by agents of ''News of the World''.  Victims included members of parliament from all three parties and including cabinet ministers.<ref name=GuardianGag20090708/>
* "The Metropolitan Police took the controversial decision not to inform the public figures whose phones had been targeted and the [[Crown Prosecution Service]] decided not to take News Group executives to court."<ref name=GuardianCoulson20090708/>
* Statements by executives misled a Parliamentary select committee, the Press Complaints Commission and the public about the extent of their newspaper's illegal acquisition of confidential information.<ref name=GuardianGag20090708/>

A chorus of denials followed.

===Metropolitan Police/Scotland Yard===
Later on the same day the ''Guardian'' articles were published, [[Metropolitan Police Service]] Commissioner [[Paul Stephenson (police officer)|Sir Paul Stephenson]] asked Assistant Commissioner [[John Yates (police officer)|John Yates]] to take a fresh look at the phone hacking to see if it should be reopened in the light of these allegations.  Yates reportedly took just eight hours to consult with senior detectives and Crown Prosecution lawyers to conclude there was no fresh material that could lead to further convictions.<ref>{{cite news|last=Wilson|first=Cherry|title=John Yates expresses 'massive regret' over phone hacking investigation|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2011/jul/09/john-yates-massive-regret-phone-hacking-investigation|accessdate=23 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=9 July 2011}}</ref> His review did not include examination of possible leads from the thousands of pages of the available evidence seized in raids between 1999 and 2006.<ref name=TelegraphYates20110709>{{cite news|author1=Palmer, Alasdair  |author2=Robert Mendick |name-list-style=amp |title=John Yates: Phone hacking investigation was a 'cock up'|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/phone-hacking/8627599/John-Yates-Phone-hacking-investigation-was-a-cock-up.html|accessdate=23 September 2011|newspaper=The Telegraph|date=9 July 2011}}</ref>

In response to emerging evidence that illegal acquisition of confidential information was more widespread than had been acknowledged by news organisations and the police, Parliamentary committees held hearings.  In September 2009, Yates maintained his position to the Commons [[Culture, Media and Sport Committee]] saying, "There remain now insufficient grounds or evidence to arrest or interview anyone else and...no additional evidence has come to light.<ref name=ParliamentYates20110902>{{cite news|title=Examination of Witnesses (Question Numbers 1889–1899)-Assistant Commissioner John Yates and Detective Chief Superintendent Philip Williams|url=https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm200910/cmselect/cmcumeds/362/9090214.htm|accessdate=27 August 2011|publisher=UK Parliament|date=2 September 2009}}</ref> Upon review of the first inquiry, he concluded that there were "hundreds, not thousands" of potential victims."<ref name=GuardianCorrupt20110707/> Yates told the Committee, "It is very few, it is a handful" of persons that had been subject to message interception.<ref name=ParliamentYates20110902a/> Although Yates was aware of the [[News International phone hacking scandal reference lists#Key evidentiary documents|"Transcript for Neville"]] email that clearly indicated more than a single rogue reporter was involved, he did not choose to interview [[Neville Thurlbeck]] about it.  Further, Yates did not choose to interview other journalists at ''[[News of the World]]'' that [[Glenn Mulcaire]] may have worked with or to look into the cases of victims beyond the eight that were pursued in 2006.<ref name=ParliamentYates20110902a>{{cite news|title=Examination of Witnesses (Question Numbers 1900–1919)-Assistant Commissioner John Yates and Detective Chief Superintendent Philip Williams|url=https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm200910/cmselect/cmcumeds/362/9090215.htm|accessdate=27 August 2011|publisher=UK Parliament|date=2 September 2009}}</ref><ref name=GuardianYates20110127>{{cite news|title=Phone hacking: Transcript of MPs questioning Met police in 2009|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jan/27/transcript-mps-question-police-phone-hacking|accessdate=23 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=27 January 2011}}</ref> The Committee's findings, released in February 2010, were critical of the police for not pursuing "evidence that merited a wider investigation."<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/><ref name=ParliamentCMSC20100209/>

Mr. Yates returned the Committee 24 March 2011 and defended his prior representations that only 10 to 12 victims had been identified based upon the criteria given to police by the [[Crown Prosecution Service]] (CPS).  The CPS denied that what they had told the Met could be reasonably used to limit the scope of Yates investigation.<ref>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=Phone hacking: Metropolitan police chief keeps up row with DPP|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/mar/24/phone-hacking-metropolitan-police-dpp|accessdate=17 September 2012|newspaper=The Guardian|date=24 March 2011}}</ref> Further, they claimed to have been misled by the Met during consultations on how broadly to investigate during the Royal Household/Goodman inquiry. Met officials reportedly "didn't discuss certain evidence with senior prosecutors, including the notes suggesting the involvement of other reporters"<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/>

The [[Home Affairs Select Committee]] also questioned assistant commissioner Yates in 2009 about the Met's continuing decision not to reopen the investigation "following allegations that 27 other [[News International]] reporters had commissioned private investigators to carry out tasks, some of which might have been illegal." Mr. Yates responded that he had only looked into the facts of the original 2006 inquiry in Goodman.<ref name=RegisterTaylor20090715>{{cite news|last=Leyden|first=John|title=MPs shown 'email evidence' of wider NotW snooping alert print tweet'One bad apple' defence wormed into|url=https://www.theregister.co.uk/2009/07/15/notw_hack_hearings/|accessdate=27 September 2011|newspaper=The Register|date=15 July 2009}}</ref> As information continued to emerge from court cases and investigative reporting, the Home Affairs Committee initiated another inquiry on 1 September 2010.  The Committee again received evidence from the Met, newspaper journalists and executives, Like the House of Commons Committee, this House of Lord's Committee also published a report highly critical of the Met, stating in part, "The difficulties were offered to us as justifying a failure to investigate further, and we saw nothing that suggested there was a real will to tackle and overcome those obstacles."  Member of Parliament [[Chris Bryant]] directly accused assistant commissioner Yates of misleading two parliamentary committees and of failing to correct itself to Parliament after errors in testimony became apparent to him.<ref name=GuardianRees20110311/>

''[[The Guardian]]'' newspaper continued to be critical of Yates, who responded to these accusations by hiring a well known libel firm that threatened legal action against various media outlets for reporting that he had misled Parliament."<ref name=GuardianRees20110311/> Yates legal fees were reportedly paid by the Met.<ref name=GuardianYates20110825>{{cite news|last=Laville|first=Sandra|title=Scotland Yard paid John Yates's legal bills|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2011/aug/25/met-yates-legal-bills|accessdate=25 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=25 August 2011}}</ref> Eventually, as queries continued to come in from celebrities and politicians asking if they had been victims of hacking, Yates directed that the evidence from the Mulcaire raid that had been stored in garbage bags for three years be entered into a computer database. Ten people were assigned this task.  Yates himself did not look at the evidence saying later, "I'm not going to go down and look at bin bags. I am supposed to be an Assistant Commissioner."<ref name=TelegraphYates20110709/> He did not re-open the investigation.

===Press Complaints Commission (PCC)===
The [[Press Complaints Commission|UK Press Complaints Commission (PCC)]] is an industry organisation charged with self-regulation.  After the conviction of Stephen Whittamore in 2005, the Information Commission, which is responsible for policing confidential databases, urged the Press Complaints Commission to issue "a clear public statement warning journalists and editors of the very real risks of committing criminal offences." Documents released under the Freedom of Information Act show that the PCC, which is funded by news media organisations, resisted doing this and finally produced guidance which the Information Commission publicly described as "disappointing".<ref name=GuardianCoulson20090708/>

The PCC's inquiry into phone hacking in 2007 concluded that phone message tapping should stop but that "there is a legitimate place for the use of subterfuge when there are grounds in the public interest to use it and it is not possible to obtain information through other means."<ref>{{cite news|title=PCC Report on Subterfuge and Newsgathering|url=http://www.pcc.org.uk/assets/218/PCC_subterfuge_report.pdf|accessdate=25 August 2011|publisher=Press Complaints Commission|date=May 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120126173046/http://www.pcc.org.uk/assets/218/PCC_subterfuge_report.pdf|archive-date=26 January 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Preston|first=Peter|title=PCC editors failed to sound the phone-hacking alarm|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/feb/06/phone-hacking-press-complaints-commission-comment|accessdate=20 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=6 February 2011}}</ref> ''[[News of the World]]'' editor [[Colin Myler]] told the PCC that Goodman's hacking was "aberrational", "a rogue exception," done by a single journalist. [[Sir Christopher Meyer]], then chairman of the PCC, "promised to investigate 'the entire newspaper and magazine industry of the UK to establish what is their practice' but opted not to question Andy Coulson on the grounds that he had resigned, and not to question any other journalist or editorial executive on the paper, apart from Myler, who necessarily had no direct knowledge of what had been going on before his arrival. The PCC's subsequent report failed to uncover any evidence of any phone hacking by any media organisation beyond that revealed at Goodman's trial."<ref name=GuardianCoulson20090708/>

The PCC's inquiry in 2009 "was concerned with whether the PCC was misled by the ''[[News of the World]]'' during its 2007 investigation, and whether there was any evidence that phone message hacking has taken place since 2007." Its report concluded the PCC was not misled and that there was no evidence of ongoing phone hacking.<ref>{{cite news|title=PCC report on phone message tapping allegations|url=http://www.pcc.org.uk/news/index.html?article=NjAyOA==|accessdate=25 August 2011|publisher=Press Complaints Commission|date=9 November 2009|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110902132404/http://pcc.org.uk/news/index.html?article=NjAyOA==|archivedate=2 September 2011|df=dmy-all}}</ref> This report and its conclusions were withdrawn on 6 July 2011, two days after ''[[The Guardian]]'' reported on the hacking of Milly Dowler's phone.<ref name=GuardianVerdicts20100224/><ref name="Press Complaints Commission">{{cite news|title=Statement from the PCC on phone hacking following meeting today (6 July 2011)|url=http://www.pcc.org.uk/news/index.html?article=NzI0Mg==|accessdate=25 August 2011|publisher=Press Complaints Commission|date=6 July 2011|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110910073940/http://www.pcc.org.uk/news/index.html?article=NzI0Mg%3D%3D|archivedate=10 September 2011|df=dmy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Letter from Baroness Buscombe to John Whittingdale|url=http://www.parliament.uk/documents/commons-committees/culture-media-and-sport/PH21-Baroness-Buscombe-to-Chairman.pdf|accessdate=26 August 2011|publisher=Press Complaints Commission|date=26 July 2011}}</ref> The organisation's future was placed in doubt as a result of its failure to address the phone hacking scandal as it unfolded.

===News Corporation===
[[File:News Internaltional Building in London.JPG|thumb|By mid-2012, formal charges had been filed against many News International journalists and executives, including former chief executive [[Rebekah Brooks]].]]

The day in 2005 that the Met seized documents from Goodman and Mulcaire and arrested them for conspiracy to intercept communications without lawful authority, ''[[News of the World]]'' editors said they were stunned and vowed to conduct an internal investigation.<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/> According to [[Colin Myler]]'s subsequent statement at the Commons [[Culture, Media and Sport Committee]] hearing, the firm of Burton Copeland was engaged in August 2005 "to absolutely oversee the investigation to cooperate with police...a very thorough investigation took place where there was a thorough review of everything from how cash payments were processed." [[Tom Crone (barrister)|Tom Crone]] testified that "Burton Copeland were in the office virtually every day...their remit was that they were brought in to go over everything and find out what had gone wrong, to liaise with the police&nbsp;... They were given absolutely free-range to ask whatever they wanted to ask." [[Andy Coulson]] testified that "I brought in Burton Copeland&nbsp;... to do an investigation. We opened up the files as much as we could. There was nothing they asked for that they were not given."  However, no report was issued covering Burton Copeland's findings, and News International never waived privilege with respect to the law firm so that they could say for themselves what they had been able to do.<ref name=NYTimesParliamentaryDocuments>{{cite news|title=Parliamentary Documents Released in Tabloid Hacking Case|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2011/08/16/world/europe/17Hacking-Documents.html|accessdate=16 August 2011|newspaper=The New York Times|date=16 August 2011}}</ref> [[Linklaters]] replaced Burton Copeland in representing News International in July 2011 and sent a letter to the Commons Culture, Media and Sport Committee in August 2011 stating "Burton Copeland did not conduct an investigation into phone hacking at the ''News of the World'' and their role was 'only about helping the police'... [but] Scotland Yard received 'very little material' from News International and Burton Copeland."<ref>{{cite news|author1=Winnett, Robert  |author2=Heidi Blake |name-list-style=amp |title=Phone hacking: first inquiry was nothing of the sort, MPs are told|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/phone-hacking/8707981/Phone-hacking-first-inquiry-was-nothing-of-the-sort-MPs-are-told.html|accessdate=27 August 2011|newspaper=The Telegraph|date=18 August 2011}}</ref>

News International employees Jonathan Chapman and Daniel Cloke, respectively the heads of the legal and human resources departments, were asked to review a limited number of emails which were made available to them "through an electronic folder of emails assembled by News International's IT department". They were asked to determine whether the emails contained evidence that others at News International were aware of Clive Goodman's illegal activity or that others themselves were engaged in similar activity. Within this limited mandate, Chapman and Cloke found no such evidence. Chapman stated they were not "tasked with looking for evidence of any other potentially illegal activities."<ref name=TelegraphChapman20110811>{{cite news|last=Chapman|first=Jonathan|title=Letter From Jonathan Chapman to Chairman, 11 August|url=http://s.telegraph.co.uk/graphics/viewer.html?doc=231986-letter-from-jonathan-chapman-to-chairman-11-august|accessdate=27 August 2011|newspaper=The Telegraph|date=11 August 2011}}</ref> The names of the individuals who selected the emails that Chapman and Cloke reviewed and the criteria used to select them were never publicly disclosed.

Some of these emails were subsequently made available to [[Harbottle & Lewis]] for review.  As with the Chapman and Cloke, News International strictly constrained the law firm's mandate to determine whether these emails contained evidence that others at News International were aware of Clive Goodman's illegal phone hacking activity or were themselves engaged in similar activity.<ref name=NYTimesParliamentaryDocuments/> This inquiry specifically did not include reviewing email traffic between Goodman and several other key senior reporters and editorial executives, current and former, at the ''News of the World'', emails to and from Mulcaire, and staff interviews and a review of cash payments. It also did not ask the reviewers to consider whether there was other evidence of criminal activity, such as making payments to serving police officers.<ref name=TelegraphChapman20110811/> Within that limited mandate, Harbottle & Lewis could report that no evidence of phone hacking beyond that arranged by Goodman was found.

These limited and controlled investigations became the basis for News International's persistently maintaining that phone hacking was not widespread but instead the work of a single "rogue reporter" and his private investigator, namely Goodman and Mulcaire.

The House of Commons Culture, Media and Sport Committee held hearings regarding phone hacking by news media companies in March 2007, in July 2009, and again in July 2011. The 2007 inquiry regarding "Privacy and media intrusion" began shortly after Goodman and Mulcaire were sentenced. It was focused on activity at ''News of the World''. On 6 March 2007, the then executive chairman of News International, [[Les Hinton]], assured the Committee that a "full, rigorous internal inquiry" had been carried out and, to his knowledge, Goodman was the only person at ''News of the World'' that knew about hacking. Hinton said, "I believe absolutely that [[Andy Coulson]] did not have knowledge of what was going on."<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/><ref name=ParliamentCMSC20100209>{{cite web|title=Press standards, privacy and libel- Second Report of Session 2009–10 Volume I Report, together with formal minutes|url=https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm200910/.../362/362i.pdf|work=Press standards, privacy and libel|publisher=UK Parliament- Culture, Media and Sport Committee|accessdate=15 October 2011|date=9 February 2010}}</ref> Asked whether Goodman was the only person who knew about the phone hacking, Hinton replied that he believed Goodman was.<ref name=GuardianCoulson20090708/>

In addition to Hinton, the Committee heard from [[Stuart Kuttner]], managing editor of the ''News of the World'', [[Tom Crone (barrister)|Tom Crone]], legal manager of News International, [[Colin Myler]], editor of ''[[News of the World]]'', and Andy Coulson, former editor of ''News of the World''. All of them stated there had been a thorough investigation of phone hacking and no evidence had ever been found that anyone besides Goodman and Mulcaire was involved.<ref name=GuardianCMSS20110719>{{cite news|title=James and Rupert Murdoch at the Culture, Media and Sport Select Committee – full transcript|newspaper=The Guardian|date=19 July 2011}}</ref>

Two years later, prompted by allegations in the three articles published by ''[[The Guardian]]'' in early July 2009, the Committee convened new hearings. Chairman [[John Whittingdale]] questioned whether the Committee had been misled by News International executives who testified two years before that Goodman and Mulcaire acted alone. The Committee again heard evidence from [[Les Hinton]], by then chief executive officer of [[Dow Jones & Company]], and Coulson, by then director of communications for the Conservative Party.  They also heard from Met assistant commissioner [[John Yates (police officer)|John Yates]] and Detective chief superintendent Philip Williams.  The Committee's findings, released in February 2010, were critical of [[News International]] executives for their "collective amnesia" and critical of the police for not pursuing "evidence that merited a wider investigation".<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/><ref name=ParliamentCMSC20100209/> Their report concluded that it was "inconceivable" that no one else, apart from Goodman, knew about the extent of phone hacking at the paper, and that the Committee had "repeatedly encountered an unwillingness to provide the detailed information that we sought, claims of ignorance or lack of recall and deliberate obfuscation".

===Acknowledgements of hacking===
While news media companies were vehemently denying that phone hacking was widespread, some of their current and former journalists who had first-hand knowledge were publicly acknowledging that it was.

In December 2010, ''[[The Guardian]]'' reported that more than 20 journalists who worked for ''[[News of the World]]'' had told ''The Guardian'', ''[[The New York Times]]'' or [[Dispatches (TV series)|Channel 4's ''Dispatches'']] that "illegal activity assisted by private investigators was commonplace and well known to executives, including editor [[Andy Coulson]]."<ref name=GuardianMiller20101215/>

It was evident from the 2005 convictions of Steve Whittamore, John Boyall, and others that illegal acquisition of confidential information for British news media organisations had been commonplace in the past.<ref name=GuardianGuilty20050416>{{cite news|author1=Cozens, Claire  |author2=Chris Tryhorn |name-list-style=amp |title=Police data sold to newspapers|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2005/apr/16/pressandpublishing.crime|accessdate=19 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=16 April 2005}}</ref><ref name=CouriermailLeigh>{{cite news|title=Guardian editor admits to hacking|url=http://www.couriermail.com.au/ipad/guardian-editor-admits-to-hacking/story-fn6ck55c-1226109505196|accessdate=15 August 2011|newspaper=Courier Mail|date=6 August 2011|archive-date=22 September 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120922143845/http://www.couriermail.com.au/ipad/guardian-editor-admits-to-hacking/story-fn6ck55c-1226109505196|url-status=dead}}</ref> Guilty pleas by [[Clive Goodman]] and [[Glenn Mulcaire]] in 2007 confirmed the practice was ongoing.<ref name=GuardianGoodman20061120/> In 2007, [[Piers Morgan]] asserted that phone hacking was common practice. "Loads of newspaper journalists were doing it. Clive Goodman, the ''[[News of the World]]'' reporter, has been made the scapegoat for a widespread practice."<ref name=IndependentWidespread20110718>{{cite news|author1=Moore, James  |author2=Ian Burrell |name-list-style=amp |title=Hacking was endemic at the 'Mirror', says former reporter|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/media/press/hacking-was-endemic-at-the-mirror-says-former-reporter-2319039.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220618/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/media/press/hacking-was-endemic-at-the-mirror-says-former-reporter-2319039.html |archive-date=18 June 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|accessdate=23 August 2011|newspaper=The Independent|date=18 July 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Robinson|first=James|title=Piers Morgan under pressure to return to UK from America|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/aug/04/piers-morgan-under-pressure-phone-hacking|accessdate=25 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=4 August 2011}}</ref> [[Andrew Neil]] former editor of ''[[The Sunday Times]]'' and former writer for the ''[[Daily Mail]]'' claimed that phone hacking "was systemic throughout the News of the World, and to a lesser extent ''[[The Sun (United Kingdom)|The Sun]]''."<ref>{{cite news|last=Dodd|first=Vikram|title=Ex-Murdoch editor Andrew Neil: News of the World revelations one of most significant media stories of our time|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2009/jul/09/andrew-neil-murdoch-andy-coulson|accessdate=1 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=9 July 2009}}</ref> [[Sharon Marshall]] former TV editor for ''[[News of the World]]'' and contributor to ''[[The Sun (United Kingdom)|The Sun]]'' said hacking was industry wide.<ref name="NYTimesRoyals20100901"/><ref name=NewYorkTimesScandal20110810>{{cite news|title=Anatomy of the News International Scandal|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2010/09/01/magazine/05tabloid-timeline.html|accessdate=31 August 2011|newspaper=The New York Times|date=10 August 2011}}</ref><ref name=GuardianCoulson20100905>{{cite news|last=Doward, Jamie and Toby Helm and Paul Harris|title=David Cameron and Andy Coulson: the PM, the PR guru and a scandalous lapse of judgment|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2010/sep/05/andy-coulson-phone-hacking-allegations|accessdate=1 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=5 September 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=Andy Coulson discussed phone hacking at News of the World, report claims|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2010/sep/01/andy-coulson-phone-hacking-allegations|accessdate=31 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=1 September 2010}}</ref> In 2010, Paul McMullan formally of ''[[News of the World]]'', not only freely acknowledged that he and others hacked phones, but maintained that doing so was justified by the public interest.<ref name="NYTimesMcMullan201111"/><ref name=GuardianMcMullen20101008>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=Phone hacking was rife at News of the World, claims new witness|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2010/sep/08/phone-hacking-news-of-the-world-witness|accessdate=20 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=8 September 2010}}</ref> ''[[The New York Times]]'' reported that "a dozen former reporters said in interviews that hacking was pervasive at ''[[News of the World]]''. "Everyone knew," one longtime reporter said. 'The office cat knew'...[[Andy Coulson]] talked freely with colleagues about the dark arts, including hacking. 'I've been to dozens if not hundreds of meetings with Andy' when the subject came up, said [a] former editor... When Coulson would ask where a story came from, editors would reply, 'We've pulled the phone records' or 'I've listened to the phone messages.'<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/>

===Civil suits===
In 2005, [[Mark Lewis (solicitor)|Mark Lewis]], solicitor for the Professional Footballers' Association, suspected that ''[[News of the World]]'' hacked phones to get information for a proposed story concerning [[Gordon Taylor (footballer)|Gordon Taylor]].<ref name="Bowcott">{{cite news|last=Bowcott|first=Owen|title='No-win, no-fee' brought down News of the World, says hacking victims' lawyer|url=https://www.theguardian.com/law/2011/jul/19/no-win-no-fee-phone-hacking|accessdate=25 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=19 July 2011}}</ref> His beliefs were confirmed late 2007 at Mulcaire's judicial proceedings, at which Mulcaire pleaded guilty and apologised to Taylor and seven others for accessing their voicemail messages.  Lewis sued ''News of the World'' on behalf of Taylor, and filed actions with the court to obtain relevant documents.  As a result, on 27 June 2008, the court ordered that documents held by the Metropolitan Police that had been obtained in the raids on Mulcaire and Steve Whittamore be turned over to Lewis.  One of these documents was the [[News International phone hacking scandal reference lists#Key evidentiary documents|"Transcript for Neville"]] email.  This document, which had been in the Met's possession for several years, clearly indicated that ''[[News of the World]]'' journalists besides Clive Goodman had been involved in phone hacking.  Public disclosure of this document would decisively contradict what [[News International]] executives had been maintaining since 2006 and open the door to hundreds if not thousands of additional lawsuits.  Within 24 hours, ''News of the World'' began settlement discussions.<ref name=NYTimesRoyals20100901/> Taylor ultimately received £700,000, and Lewis became the first solicitor to win a settlement from the newspaper for phone hacking.<ref name="Bowcott"/> The amount of the settlement suggested more was at stake to News International than liability for phone hacking.  The agreement included non-disclosure clauses that prevented release of information that would confirm more than one ''[[News of the World]]'' journalist was involved in illegally acquiring confidential information.  This effectively prevented other potential litigants from learning that phone hacking was more widespread.

[[James Murdoch]], then a senior executive at [[News International]], later denied he had been aware of the "Transcript For Neville" email when he agreed to the generous settlement.  He denied that he had reason to believe there was more than one reporter involved in phone hacking at News International's publications.<ref name=GuardianNeville20110722/><ref name=ParliamentYates20110902/><ref name="Leigh, David and Vikram Dodd"/><ref>{{cite news|title=James and Rupert Murdoch at the Culture, Media and Sport Select Committee – full transcript|url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/datablog/2011/jul/20/james-rupert-murdoch-full-transcript|accessdate=19 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian- DataBlog|date=19 July 2011|first1=Ami|last1=Sedghi|first2=Simon|last2=Rogers}}</ref> He continued to maintain through late 2010 that the hacking at his newspaper was the work of a single reporter, Clive Goodman.<ref name=GuardianCMSS20110719/>

However, [[Tom Crone (barrister)|Tom Crone]] and [[Colin Myler]], respectively the newspaper's legal advisor and editor, claimed they had met with James Murdoch and indicated to him the significance of the email, and it was this that resulted in agreement among them to make a large settlement payment to Taylor.<ref name=ParliamentCrone20110816>{{cite news|title=Committee publishes further written evidence on phone-hacking on 16 August|url=http://www.parliament.uk/business/committees/committees-a-z/commons-select/culture-media-and-sport-committee/news/further-news-international-correspondence/|accessdate=12 September 2011|publisher=UK Parliament|date=16 August 2011}}</ref> Crone had received the email about 12 May 2008 and promptly discussed it with Myler.
