Julian Pike, a partner at [[Farrer & Co]] who represented the [[News Group Newspapers]] subsidiary of [[News International]] during the settlement negotiations claimed that he had informed News International of evidence suggesting "a powerful case" could be made that three ''[[News of the World]]'' journalists had illegally accessed confidential information.  Pike also claimed that Colin Myler met with James Murdoch on 27 May 2008, after Pike had received a copy of the new evidence which had been emailed by [[Tom Crone]] to Myler. This meeting was in addition to Myler's subsequent meeting with Murdoch and Crone 10 June 2008.<ref>{{cite news|last=Robinson|first=James|title=Phone hacking: NI lawyer says he knew its 'rogue reporter' defence was wrong|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/oct/19/phone-hacking-lawyer-ni-rogue-reporter|accessdate=19 October 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=19 October 2011}}</ref> On 7 June 2008, Colin Myler sent an email to James Murdoch advising that the situation with the Gordon Taylor was "as bad as we feared."  Included at the end of Myler's comments was an email to Myler from Crone that refers to a "nightmare scenario" and to the "Ross Hindley email," aka the "Transcript For Neville."  Included at the end of this email was an email to Crone from Pike stating that Taylor wants to demonstrate that "what happened to him is/was rife throughout the organisation [and] to correct the paper telling Parliament inquiries that this was not happening when it was."  Murdoch claimed he did not read the email in its entirety and therefore did not grasp the implications that more than one "rogue reporter" was involved in phone hacking at ''[[News of the World]]''.<ref>{{cite news|author1=Sabbagh, Dan  |author2=Mark Sweney |name-list-style=amp |title=James Murdoch: I didn't read crucial phone-hacking email|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/dec/13/james-murdoch-phone-hacking-email|date=13 December 2011|accessdate=8 May 2012}}</ref><ref name=GuardianMylerEmail>{{cite news|title=James Murdoch, Colin Myler and Tom Crone emails – full text|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/interactive/2011/dec/13/james-murdoch-tom-crone-colin-myler|date=13 December 2011|accessdate=8 May 2012}}</ref>

The settlement with Taylor remained secret until it was reported by ''[[The Guardian]]'' in early July 2009 in one of the three articles relating to phone hacking.<ref name=GuardianGag20090708/> Days later, [[Max Clifford]], another of the eight victims named in the 2006 indictment of Mulcaire, announced his intentions to sue.  In March 2010, [[News International]] agreed to settle his suit for £1,000,000, again a larger than expected settlement if only hacking Clifford's phone was the issue.<ref name=GuardianClifford20100309>{{cite news|author1=Davies, Nick  |author2=Rob Evans |name-list-style=amp |title=Max Clifford drops News of the World phone hacking action in £1m deal|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2010/mar/09/clifford-news-of-the-world-phone-hacking|accessdate=20 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=9 March 2010}}</ref> These awards encouraged other possible victims and their solicitors to explore possibilities, resulting in more and more queries to the Metropolitan Police about whether their names were on Mulcaire's lists.  Responses from the Met were difficult to obtain. Solicitor Charlotte Harris, who represented Clifford, wrote to the Metropolitan Police about other of her clients, [[Leslie Ash]] and her husband [[Lee Chapman]],  "asking whether they had also been hacked.  The police took three months to reply."<ref>{{cite news|title=Charlotte Harris: Nowhere to hide, says the lawyer on Murdoch's case|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/profiles/charlotte-harris-nowhere-to-hide-says-the-lawyer-on-murdochs-case-2269242.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220618/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/profiles/charlotte-harris-nowhere-to-hide-says-the-lawyer-on-murdochs-case-2269242.html |archive-date=18 June 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|accessdate=26 September 2011|newspaper=The Independent|date=18 April 2010}}</ref>

George and Richard Rebh, owners of FLOORgraphics filed suit in 2006 against [[News Corporation (1980–2013)|News Corp.'s]] US advertising subsidiary News America Marketing that, based upon forensic evidence, News America had engaged in illegal computer espionage against in 2006 by breaking into FLOORgraphics' password-protected computer system and obtaining proprietary information at least eleven times.  It was alleged that this illegal acquisition of confidential business information was part of "a prolonged and concerted effort to destroy (FLOORgraphics)."  The issue came to trial in 2009.  A whistle-blower from News Corp. was prepared to give supporting testimony. Before his testimony was given, News America Marketing settled the case by purchasing FLOORgraphics from its owners for about $30&nbsp;million. This settlement included a "non-disparagement" clause that effectively required the Rebhs to keep quiet about the case.  The purchase price appeared excessive in contrast to FLOORgraphics' earnings at the time of about $1&nbsp;million a year.  A business law professor commented at the time that this price indicated how worried News Corp. was about the lawsuit and the substantial legal risk the suit presented to News Corp.<ref>{{cite news|last=Caroom|first=Eliot|title=Alleged computer hacking of N.J. company by News Corp. subsidiary gets new attention|url=http://www.nj.com/business/index.ssf/2011/07/alleged_computer_hacking_of_nj.html|accessdate=19 August 2011|newspaper=The Star-Ledger|date=18 July 2011}}</ref>

In spite of settlements that prohibited disclosure of illegal activity, information disclosed through judicial activity prompted other victims to pursue financial damages.  One commentator observed that "the Goodman-Mulcaire revelations and subsequent prosecution were supposed to have settled the hacking matter forever and might have done just that, except that successful law suits...  kept popping up against [News of the World] after the convictions.'<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.thefeministwire.com/2011/07/29/dial-m-for-murdoch-and-mayhem/ |title=Dial M for Murdoch and Mayhem |author=Spillers, Hortense |work=The Feminist Wire |date=29 July 2011 |accessdate=12 August 2011}}</ref>

===More investigative reporting===
On 15 December 2011, ''[[The Guardian]]'' published an article authored by [[Nick Davies]] disclosing that documents, seized from the home of private investigator [[Glenn Mulcaire]] by [[Metropolitan Police Service]] in 2006 and only recently made available to the public by court action, implied that ''[[News of the World]]'' editor [[Ian Edmondson]] specifically instructed Mulcaire to intercept voice messages of [[Sienna Miller]], [[Jude Law]], and several others. The documents also implied that Mulcaire was engaged by others at ''News of the World'', including chief reporter [[Neville Thurlbeck]] and assistant editor [[Greg Miskiw]], who had then worked directly for editor [[Andy Coulson]].  This contradicted testimony to the [[Culture, Media and Sport Committee]] by newspaper executives and senior Met officials that Mulcaire acted on his own and that there was no evidence of hacking by other than him and a single "rogue reporter," namely [[Clive Goodman]]. Within five weeks of this article appearing, [[Ian Edmondson|Ian Edmundson]] was suspended from ''News of the World'',<ref>{{cite news|author1=Robinson, James  |author2=Vikram Dodd |name-list-style=amp |title=Andy Coulson resignation: Private eye's court claims sealed fate|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jan/21/glenn-mulcaire-edmondson-coulson-resignation|accessdate=21 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=21 January 2011}}</ref> [[Andy Coulson]] resigned as Chief Press Secretary to David Cameron,<ref name=GuardianVerdicts20100224/><ref name=TelegraphCoulson20110121>{{cite news|title=Andy Coulson quits Number 10|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/politics/david-cameron/8274940/Andy-Coulson-quits-Number-10.html|accessdate=20 August 2011|newspaper=The Telegraph|date=21 January 2011}}</ref> the [[Crown Prosecution Service]] began a review of evidence it had,<ref>{{cite news|last=Washbrook.|first=Cyril|title=UK: Prosecutor orders review of phone-hacking evidence|url=http://www.mediaspy.org/report/2011/01/15/uk-prosecutor-orders-review-of-phone-hacking-evidence/|accessdate=12 October 2011|newspaper=Media Spy- The Spy Report|date=15 January 2011|archive-date=10 September 2012|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120910162538/http://www.mediaspy.org/report/2011/01/15/uk-prosecutor-orders-review-of-phone-hacking-evidence/|url-status=dead}}</ref> and the Met renewed its investigation into phone hacking, something it had declined to do since 2007.<ref name=GuardianMiller20101215>{{cite news|last=Davies|first=Nick|title=Phone hacking approved by top News of the World executive: New files|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2010/dec/15/phone-hacking-sienna-miller-evidence|accessdate=11 October 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=15 December 2010}}</ref>

==Renewed investigations (2011–2012)==
{{Update section|date=August 2026}}
During this period, revelations of unpopular invasions of privacy inflamed public opinion, leading to resignations of senior journalists, media executives and police officials and to reinvigorated investigations of wrongdoing.

===Operations Weeting, Tuleta, and Elveden===
The first renewed Met investigation was titled [[Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal#Operation Weeting (2011): interception of voicemail|Operation Weeting]] and began in January 2011.  It was focused on the illegal interception of voicemail .  Between 45 and 60 officers began looking over the 11,000 pages of evidence seized from Mulcaire back in August 2006.<ref>{{cite news|author1=Milmo, Cahal  |author2=Martin Hickman |name-list-style=amp |title=Freelance reporter held in phone-hacking investigation|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/crime/freelance-reporter-held-in-phonehacking-investigation-2302079.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220618/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/crime/freelance-reporter-held-in-phonehacking-investigation-2302079.html |archive-date=18 June 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|accessdate=12 October 2011|newspaper=The Independent|date=24 June 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Laville|first=Sandra|title=Phone hacking: police make another arrest|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/sep/07/phone-hacking-police-make-arrest|accessdate=17 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=7 September 2011}}</ref> By mid-year, five people were arrested, including senior journalists from ''[[News of the World]]''.

In June 2011, the long-ignored issue of computer hacking was addressed by the launching of [[Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal#Operation Tuleta (2011): computer hacking|Operation Tuleta]].

Having failed thus far to put the phone hacking issue to rest, [[News International]]'s law firm, Hickman & Rose, now hired former [[Director of Public Prosecutions]] [[Ken Macdonald]] to review the emails that News International executives had used as the basis of their claim that no one at ''[[News of the World]]'' but [[Clive Goodman]] had been involved in phone hacking.  Macdonald immediately concluded, regardless of whether others had been involved, that there was clear evidence of criminal activity, including payments to serving police officers.   Macdonald arranged for this evidence to be turned over to the Met, which led to their opening in July 2011 [[Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal#Operation Elveden (2011): bribery, corruption|Operation Elveden]], an investigation focused on bribery and corruption within the Met's ranks.

On 4 July 2011, the phone hacking scandal broke wide upon with publication of ''[[The Guardian]]'s'' article titled "Missing Milly Dowler's voicemail was hacked by News of the World" authored by [[Nick Davies]] and Amelia Hill.<ref name=GuardianDowler20110704>{{cite news|author1=Davies, Nick  |author2=Amelia Hill |name-list-style=amp |title=Missing Milly Dowler's voicemail was hacked by News of the World|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2011/jul/04/milly-dowler-voicemail-hacked-news-of-world|accessdate=20 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=4 July 2011}}</ref> This article disclosed to the public for the first time that voicemail messages from [[Milly Dowler]]'s phone had been hacked back in 2002 by an agent of ''[[News of the World]]''.<ref name=GuardianDowler20120509>{{cite news|last=Leigh|first=David|title=Milly Dowler: truth about deletion of messages may never be known|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2012/may/09/milly-dowler-deletion-messages|date=9 May 2012|accessdate=9 May 2012}}</ref> This disclosure inflamed public opinion and led to loss of advertising for ''News of the World'' and subsequent closure of this 168-year-old newspaper.  The denials of widespread hacking made by media executives and senior law enforcements officers were no longer tenable.  Within two weeks, senior [[News Corporation (1980–2013)|News Corporation]] executives resigned, including [[Les Hinton]], chief executive of [[Dow Jones & Company]],<ref name=GuardianHinton20110715>{{cite news|last=O'Carroll|first=Lisa|title=Les Hinton resigns from News Corp|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/15/les-hinton-rupert-murdoch|accessdate=21 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=15 July 2011}}</ref> [[Rebekah Brooks]], chief executive of [[News International]],<ref>{{cite news|last=Dowell|first=Ben|title=Rebekah Brooks resigns over phone-hacking scandal|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/15/rebekah-brooks-resigns-phone-hacking-scandal|accessdate=21 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=15 July 2011}}</ref> [[Tom Crone (barrister)|Tom Crone]], legal manager of [[News International]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/13/news-of-the-world-tom-crone-to-leave |title=News of the World legal manager Tom Crone to leave News International |author1=Sabbagh, Dan  |author2=Jane Martinson  |name-list-style=amp |work=The Guardian |date=13 July 2011 |accessdate=15 August 2011 }}</ref> and [[Lawrence Jacobs (lawyer)|Lawrence Jacobs]],<ref>{{cite news|last=Peters|first=Jeremy W.|title=General Counsel of News Corp. Resigns in Wake of Settlement|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/06/09/business/media/09newscorp.html|accessdate=11 October 2011|newspaper=The New York Times|date=8 June 2011}}</ref> general counsel for [[News Corporation (1980–2013)|News Corporation]].  Also within two weeks, the two top officials of the [[Metropolitan Police Service]] resigned, namely Commissioner [[Paul Stephenson (police officer)|Paul Stephenson]]<ref name=guardianStephenson20110818>{{cite news|last=Campbell|first=Duncan|title=Sir Paul Stephenson's resignation: the former Met boss has a tale to tell|url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2011/jul/18/paul-stephenson-met-police-resign|accessdate=27 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=18 July 2011}}</ref> and Assistant Commissioner [[John Yates (police officer)|John Yates]].<ref name=GuardianRusbridger20110717>{{cite news | author =Rusbridger, Alan| title =How We Broke the Murdoch Scandal- Guardian editor Alan Rusbridger on his dogged reporter, a U.S Ally—and a gamble that finally paid off.| work =The Daily Beast| date =17 July 2011| url =http://www.thedailybeast.com/newsweek/2011/07/17/how-the-guardian-broke-the-news-of-the-world-hacking-scandal.html| accessdate =7 August 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Dodd|first1= Vikram|last2= Jones|first2=Sam |last3=Mulholland|first3=Hélène |title=John Yates resigns from Met police over phone-hacking scandal|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2011/jul/18/john-yates-met-police-resigns-quits|accessdate=21 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=18 July 2011}}</ref>

The new Met Commissioner, [[Bernard Hogan-Howe]], took the unusual step of asking a team from an outside police force, the Durham constabulary headed by Jon Stoddart, to review the work of Operation Weeting.<ref name="Laville">{{cite news|last=Laville|first=Sandra|title=Phone hacking: Durham police called in to review evidence|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/sep/15/phone-hacking-durham-police-review|accessdate=12 October 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=15 September 2011}}</ref> By the end of the year, sixteen people, mostly editors and journalists who had at one time worked for ''[[News of the World]]'', were arrested in conjunction with recently renewed investigations of illegal acquisition of confidential information.  These included former editors [[Rebekah Brooks]],<ref name="Deans">{{cite news|last=Deans|first=Jason|title=Phone hacking: former NoW executive editor Neil Wallis arrested in London|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/14/phone-hacking-60-year-old-arrested|accessdate=21 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=14 July 2011}}</ref> and [[Andy Coulson]].<ref name="guardian.co.uk">{{cite news|last=Laville|first=Sandra|title=Andy Coulson arrested over phone-hacking allegations|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/08/andy-coulson-arrested-phone-hacking-allegations|accessdate=21 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=8 July 2011}}</ref> By the following September, the total number of arrests reached ninety and included many journalists from [[The Sun (United Kingdom)|The Sun]], another [[News International]] newspaper where Ms. Brooks had been editor.

In May 2012, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) [[News International phone hacking scandal reference lists#Charged with crimes|charged six individuals]] with conspiring to pervert the course of justice by removing documents and computers to conceal them from investigating detectives. Charged were former News International CEO [[Rebekah Brooks]], [[News International phone hacking scandal reference lists#Charged with crimes|her husband, her personal assistant, her bodyguard, her chauffeur, and the head of security at News International]].<ref name=GuardianBrooks20120515>{{cite news|last=Laville|first=Sandra|title=Rebekah Brooks charged with perverting the course of justice|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2012/may/15/rebekah-brooks-charged-perverting-course-justice|date=15 May 2012|accessdate=20 May 2012}}</ref> These charges were made about [[Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal#Operation Weeting (2011): interception of voicemail|1 year]] after the Metropolitan Police Service reopened its dormant investigation into phone hacking,<ref name=MetPoliceWeeting20110706>{{cite press release|title=Statement from Commissioner |url=http://content.met.police.uk/News/Statement-from-Commissioner/1260269177528/1257246741786 |date=6 July 2011|publisher=Metropolitan Police|accessdate=21 August 2011}}</ref> about [[Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal#The Yates review of evidence (2009)|3 years]] after the then Assistant Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police Service [[John Yates (police officer)|John Yates]] told the Commons Culture, Media and Sport Committee that "no additional evidence has come to light,"<ref name="ParliamentYates20110902"/> [[Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal#The Royal Household / Goodman inquiry (2006)|5 years]] after [[News International]] executives began claiming that phone hacking was the work of a single "rogue reporter,<ref name=GuardianRogue2012013>{{cite news|last=Sabbagh|first=Dan|title=Phone-hacking: how the 'rogue reporter' defence slowly crumbled|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/mar/13/phone-hacking-rogue-reporter-defence|date=13 March 2012|accessdate=17 July 2012}}</ref> [[Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal#Investigative reporting by newspapers|10 years]] after ''The Guardian'' began reporting that the Met had evidence of widespread illegal acquisition of confidential information,<ref name=GuardianRees20020921aB>{{cite news|last=McLagan|first=Graeme|title=Fraudster squad- Graeme McLagan on the black economy run by corrupt police and private detectives|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2002/sep/21/privacy2|accessdate=28 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=20 September 2002}}</ref> and [[Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal#Operation Nigeria (1999)|13 years]] after the Met began accumulating "boxloads" of that evidence but kept it unexamined in trash bags at Scotland Yard.<ref name="GuardianRees20110608b"/>

On 24 July 2012, [[News International phone hacking scandal reference lists#Charged with crimes|charges were brought against eight former employees or agents]] of ''[[News of the World]]'' including head editors [[Rebekah Brooks]] and [[Andy Coulson]].   All eight were charged regarding illegal interception of communications relating to specific individuals<ref name=CPS20120724>{{cite press release|title=Alison Levitt QC's announcement on charges arising from Operation Weeting|url=http://blog.cps.gov.uk/|date=24 July 2012|publisher=Crown Prosecution Service|accessdate=24 July 2012|archive-date=12 August 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110812143408/http://blog.cps.gov.uk/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=GuardianCharged20120724>{{cite news|title=Phone hacking: full list of charges|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2012/jul/24/phone-hacking-charges|date=24 July 2012|accessdate=24 July 2012}}</ref>

===Other inquiries launched===
The furore over hacking of Milly Dowler's phone energised investigative bodies. Two days after ''[[The Guardian]]'' article was published, Prime Minister [[David Cameron]] announced the establishment of the [[Leveson Inquiry]]. In the following months, [[News International phone hacking scandal reference lists#Investigations|a dozen additional investigations were launched]] into illegal acquisition of confidential information in the UK, US, and Australia.

===Additional civil suits===
As of April 2011, there were at least 24 civil suits from celebrities and politicians filed for breach of privacy against News of the World alone.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/apr/14/phone-hacking-news-corp |title=Phone-hacking saga is complex and unpredictable ... with lots of loose ends |author=Sabbagh, Dan |work=The Guardian |date=14 April 2011 |accessdate=13 April 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Lyall|first=Sarah|title=British Tabloid Accepts Blame in Cell Hacking|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/04/09/world/europe/09hacking.html?pagewanted=all|accessdate=17 August 2001|newspaper=The New York Times|date=8 April 2011}}</ref> As of early October 2011, there were reportedly 63 civil suits directed at [[News International]] relating to the phone hacking scandal.<ref name=GuardianSuits20111005>{{cite news|last=Greenslade|first=Ray|title=Phone hacking: News International faces more than 60 claims|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/oct/05/phone-hacking-news-international-60-claims?CMP=twt_gu|accessdate=5 October 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=5 October 2011}}</ref> Noting that there might be many more cases initiated over phone hacking, high court judge Mr Justice Vos selected test cases that "would enable him to decide the damages that were properly payable across a range of alleged factual situations, and make it possible for other cases to be resolved without the need for further hearings." He added that the trial would cover the issues of "what was agreed to be done, by whom, for what purpose, over what period and who was involved".<ref name=GuardianVos20110520>{{cite news|author1=Robinson, James  |author2=John Plunkett |name-list-style=amp |title=Jude Law and Chris Bryant join phone-hacking test cases|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/may/20/jude-law-chris-bryant-phone-hacking|accessdate=12 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=20 May 2011}}</ref> This opened the door to full disclosure regarding phone hacking activity, and was in stark contrast to court action in 2006, when the court was persuaded by News International to seal records that contained evidence of criminal activity.<ref name=GuardianGag20090708/>

Nicola Phillps had been assistant to [[Max Clifford]] when her phone was hacked.  Her suit against [[Glenn Mulcaire]] called for Mulcaire to disclose the name of the person who instructed him to intercept her phone messages.  Mulcaire opposed this disclosure on the grounds that doing so might force him to incriminate himself.  After a lengthy legal battle involving 20 months of appeals, the supreme court ordered him in July 2012 to disclose.<ref>{{cite news|last=Halliday|first=Josh|title=Glenn Mulcaire ordered to reveal who gave phone-hacking order|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/jul/04/glenn-mulcaire-ordered-reveal-phone-hacking|date=4 July 2012|accessdate=26 September 2012}}</ref>

As of 25 September 2012, 292 suits against [[News International]] had been filed for alleged phone hacking.  These were in addition to the 58 lawsuits settled previously and in addition to the 137 claims News International had accepted directly from victims without involving court proceeding.  Justice Vos had set a deadline of 14 September for receiving claims.<ref name=GuardianClaims20120925>{{cite news|last=O'Carroll|first=Lisa|title=Phone-hacking claims against News International near 300|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/sep/25/phone-hacking-claims-news-international|date=25 September 2012|accessdate=25 September 2012}}</ref> One suit that came in involved the husband of Justice Vos' niece.<ref name=GuardianVos20120925>{{cite news|last=O'Carroll|first=Lisa|title=Phone hacking: judge reveals relative is among claimants|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/sep/25/phone-hacking-judge-relative-claimants|date=25 September 2012|accessdate=25 September 2012}}</ref> Another suit alleged illegal acquisition of information from a mobile phone as recently as 2010.<ref name=GuardianMcDonagh201209/>

==Commercial consequences==
[[File:Rupert Murdoch - WEF Davos 2007.jpg|upright|thumb|The Corporate Library, a research firm that grades companies' governance from A to F, gave
[[Rupert Murdoch]]'s [[News Corporation (1980–2013)|News Corporation]] an F for the six years prior to the phone hacking scandal's breaking.  News Corp. reportedly got an F "only because there is no lower grade."<ref>{{cite news|last=Chittum|first=Ryan|title=Rupert Murdoch and the Corporate Culture of News Corp.|url=https://www.cjr.org/the_audit/rupert_murdoch_and_the_corpora.php|accessdate=15 September 2011|newspaper=Columbia Journalism Review- The Audit|date=27 July 2011}}</ref>]]
In the months following ''[[The Guardian]]'' article regarding Milly Dowler, the fallout from the phone hacking scandal had [[News International phone hacking scandal reference lists#Commercial consequences|many adverse commercial consequences]] for [[News Corporation (1980–2013)|News Corporation]].

''[[News of the World]]'' was shut down after 168 years in business<ref name=GuardianNotW20110807>{{cite news|last=Robinson|first=James|title=News of the World to close as Rupert Murdoch acts to limit fallout|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/07/news-of-the-world-rupert-murdoch|accessdate=28 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=7 July 2011}}</ref> and [[News Corporation (1980–2013)|News Corp.]] withdrew its $12&nbsp;billion bid for [[BSkyB|British Sky Broadcasting Group plc (BSkyB)]], reportedly the biggest reverse of [[Rupert Murdoch]]'s career.<ref>{{cite news|last=Wintour, Patrick and Dan Sabbagh and Nicholas Watt|title=Rupert Murdoch gives up BSkyB takeover bid|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/13/rupert-murdoch-gives-up-bskyb-bid|accessdate=28 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=14 July 2011}}</ref> News Corp. lost its contract bid with the NY State Comptroller over concerns about the phone-hacking scandal.<ref>{{cite news|last=Adams|first=Russell|title=News Corp. Loses Contract|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424053111904332804576539013195155444|accessdate=31 August 2011|newspaper=The Wall Street Journal|date=30 August 2011}}</ref> The legal bills and settlement of suits cost News Corp. hundreds of millions of dollars.<ref name=BostonGlobe20120508>{{cite news|title=Developments in British phone-hacking scandal|newspaper=Developments in British phone-hacking scandal|url=http://www.boston.com/business/technology/articles/2012/05/08/developments_in_british_phone_hacking_scandal/|date=8 May 2012|accessdate=9 May 2012}}{{dead link|date=May 2026|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

[[Rupert Murdoch]] endorsed [[Chase Carey]] as a future chief executive for News Corp. rather than his son [[James Murdoch]], who had been viewed as the favourite to succeed Rupert.<ref>{{cite news|last=Adegoke|first=Yinka|title=Murdoch endorses Carey as next in line|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-newscorp-idUSTRE77967X20110810|accessdate=21 October 2011|work=Reuters|date=10 August 2011}}</ref> James resigned as Chairman of British Sky Broadcasting Group (BSkyB), distancing the company from the scandal at [[News International]].<ref>{{cite news|last= Sabbagh|first=Dan, and Dominic Rushe|title=James Murdoch steps down as BSkyB chairman as hacking scandal deepens|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/apr/03/james-murdoch-step-down-bskyb-chairman|accessdate=5 May 2012|newspaper=The Guardian|date=3 April 2012}}</ref> James was harshly criticised by the British Office of Communications ([[Ofcom]]), which concluded that he "repeatedly fell short of the conduct to be expected of as a chief executive and chairman" and that his lack of action in relation to phone hacking was "difficult to comprehend and ill-judged".<ref>{{cite news|author1=O'Carroll, Lisa  |author2=Lizzy Davies |name-list-style=amp |title=Sky ruled fit for broadcast licence, but James Murdoch comes in for criticism|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/sep/20/sky-broadcast-james-murdoch-criticised|date=20 September 2012|accessdate=23 September 2012}}</ref> Rupert himself was found to be "not a fit person to exercise the stewardship of major international company" by the Commons [[Culture, Media and Sport Committee]].<ref name="Sabbagh">{{cite news|last= Sabbagh|first=Dan, and Josh Halliday|title=Rupert Murdoch 'not fit' to lead major international company, MPs conclude|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/may/01/rupert-murdoch-not-fit-select-committee|accessdate=5 May 2012|newspaper=The Guardian|date=1 May 2012}}</ref>

Eighteen major shareholders of News Corp. advised Rupert they planned to vote against him as chairman at the upcoming annual meeting of the company.<ref>{{cite news|last=Rushton|first=Katherine|title=Rupert Murdoch will find News Corp's AGM vote hard to ignore|newspaper=The Telegraph|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/newsbysector/mediatechnologyandtelecoms/media/9413233/Rupert-Murdoch-will-find-News-Corps-AGM-vote-hard-to-ignore.html|date=19 July 2012|accessdate=22 July 2012}}</ref> Several large investors in [[News Corporation (1980–2013)|News Corporation]] filed suit against members of the company's board of directorsfor alleged misconduct including "allowing Murdoch to use News Corp as his own personal fiefdom."  The complaint cited the phone hacking scandal at ''[[News of the World]]'' and tactics used by News America Marketing and NDS Group Plc that may have included "stealing computer technology, hacking into business plans and computers and violating the law through a wide range of anti-competitive behaviour".<ref>{{cite news|last=Pilkington|first=Ed|title=News Corp shareholders lodge complaint against Rupert Murdoch|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/sep/13/news-corporation-shareholders-complaint|date=13 September 2011|accessdate=22 July 2012}}</ref> The stockholders allege "failed corporate governance and domination by a controlling shareholder" who misused company resources to gain political power, and that directors "condoned Murdoch's use of News Corp to pursue his quest for power, control, and political gain" at shareholder expense.  Further, "the investors allege that board members refused to initiate a proper investigation for fear of angering Rupert Murdoch and his son, James."<ref>{{cite news|last=Greenslade|first=Roy|title=Investors accuse News Corp board of 'lax oversight'|newspaper=The Guardian- Greenslade Blog|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/greenslade/2012/jun/21/news-corporation-rupert-murdoch|date=21 June 2012|accessdate=22 June 2012}}</ref>

[[Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington]] (CREW) asked the [[Federal Communications Commission]] (FCC) to revoke the 27 Fox broadcast licenses News Corp. holds, claiming significant character deficiencies warranted disqualification since "the House of Commons report makes clear that both Rupert and James Murdoch were complicit in New Corp.'s illegal activities."<ref>{{Citation|url=http://www.citizensforethics.org/legal-filings/entry/fcc-revoke-murdoch-broadcast-licenses-news-corp-fox|title=CREW Calls for FCC to Revoke Murdoch's Broadcast Licenses|work=Legal Filings|publisher=Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW)|date=1 May 2012|accessdate=22 September 2012|archive-date=30 October 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121030083943/http://www.citizensforethics.org/legal-filings/entry/fcc-revoke-murdoch-broadcast-licenses-news-corp-fox|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The [[Church of England]] sold its £1.9m stake in News Corp.<ref>{{cite news|last=Naete|first=Rupert|title=Church of England sells News Corp shares in phone-hacking protest|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/aug/07/church-of-england-news-corp|date=7 August 2012|accessdate=7 August 2012}}</ref> "Board-level dialogue"  did not satisfy the Church that the company "had shown, or is likely in the immediate future to show, a commitment to implement necessary corporate governance reform."<ref>{{cite press release|title=Church of England disinvests from News Corporation|publisher=The Church of England|url=http://churchofengland.org/media-centre/news/2012/08/church-of-england-disinvests-from-news-corporation.aspx|date=7 August 2012|accessdate=7 August 2012}}</ref> A year earlier, the Church's Ethical Investment Advisory Group criticised "reprehensible and unethical" conduct and stated "We cannot imagine circumstances in which we would be satisfied with any outcome that does not hold senior executives to account at News Corporation for the gross failures of management at the ''News of the World''."<ref>{{cite press release|title=News Corporation: Statement from Ethical Investment Advisory Group|publisher=The Church of England|url=http://www.churchofengland.org/media-centre/news/2011/07/news-corporation-statement-from-ethical-investment-advisory-group.aspx|date=9 July 2011|accessdate=7 August 2012}}</ref>

[[John Dean]], who as White House Counsel to US President [[Richard Nixon]] helped orchestrate the [[Watergate scandal|Watergate coverup]], observed:
{{Blockquote|The unfolding scandal that is currently hammering the reputation and value of News Corp. so closely parallels the sequence of events that provoked my warning to Nixon&nbsp;... Just as Nixon did not undertake the initiating illegality himself (the bugging of the Democratic National Committee headquarters), nor did Murdoch personally undertake the illegal hacking of voice mails. Rather, both men created norms and standards within their respective organisations where such conduct was not only considered acceptable, but actually encouraged.<ref name= johndean2011-07-14>{{cite news |url=http://jhaines6.wordpress.com/2011/07/21/rupert-murdoch%E2%80%99s-watergatethe-troubling-parallels/ |title=Rupert Murdoch's Watergate:The Troubling Parallels |author=Dean, John |date=14 July 2011 |accessdate=11 August 2011 |archive-date=21 October 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111021192244/http://jhaines6.wordpress.com/2011/07/21/rupert-murdoch%E2%80%99s-watergatethe-troubling-parallels/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>}}

==Status of arrests, charges, and convictions==
In the UK, over 100 people have been arrested and many of these people charged with crimes relating to the illegal acquisition of confidential information.  All but ten of these were arrested or rearrested since the [[Metropolitan Police Service]] renewed investigations in 2011.  Deputy assistant commissioner Sue Akers, who became responsible for the Met's investigations in 2011, expressed the view in 2012 that the investigations and related prosecutions could take three more years.  As she spoke, there were 185 Met officers and civilian staff working on the Operations [[Operation Weeting|Weeting]], [[Operation Elveden|Elveden]] and [[Operation Tuleta|Tuleta]].<ref>{{cite news|author1=Deans, Jason  |author2=Lisa O'Carroll |name-list-style=amp |title=Phone-hacking investigations and prosecutions 'could take three years'|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/sep/04/phone-hacking-investigations|date=4 September 2012|accessdate=25 September 2012}}</ref>

The following table lists in alphabetical order the named individuals arrested since 1999 in conjunction with alleged illegal acquisition and trafficking of confidential information.  It shows the dates each was arrested and indicates the status of each individual's case, along with dates for formal charges made, convictions, and other outcomes, as applicable. All arrests in conjunction with the phone hacking scandal were made in the UK. Chronological lists of arrests, charges and convictions, including more details about them, are included with the [[phone hacking scandal reference lists]].

==Issues for consideration==
Even as scope of the scandal was unfolding, proposals were being debated in legislatures and in the press about whether regulatory remedies were warranted. Two days after ''[[The Guardian]]'' article regarding Milly Dowler was published, Prime Minister [[David Cameron]] announced that a public government inquiry would be initiated. Cameron named [[Brian Leveson|Lord Justice Leveson]] to chair the inquiry that would look into phone hacking at ''[[News of the World]]'' and other newspapers, the diligence of the initial police inquiry, alleged illegal payments to police by the press, and the general culture and ethics of the media, including broadcasters and [[social media]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Phone hacking: David Cameron announces terms of phone-hacking inquiry|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/phone-hacking/8634757/Phone-hacking-David-Cameron-announces-terms-of-phone-hacking-inquiry.html|accessdate=9 October 2011|newspaper=The Telegraph|date=13 July 2011}}</ref><ref name=GuardianLeveson20110906>{{cite news|last=Halliday|first=Josh|title=Phone hacking: Rebekah Brooks to give evidence to Leveson inquiry|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/sep/06/phone-hacking-rebekah-brooks-leveson|accessdate=6 September 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=6 September 2011}}</ref><ref name=GuardianLeveson20110713>{{cite news|last=Bowcott|first=Owen|title=Lord Justice Leveson: profile of phone-hacking inquiry chairman|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jul/13/lord-justice-leveson-profile-hacking|accessdate=21 August 2011|newspaper=The Guardian|date=13 July 2011}}</ref> Some of the issues the [[Leveson Inquiry]] and other investigative bodies would address are listed below.

===Performance of the Metropolitan Police Service===
{{Main|Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal}}

[[Metropolitan Police role in the News International phone hacking scandal#Criticisms and responses|The Met received severe criticism]] for its role in the phone hacking scandal.  Commentators observed that the personal relationships among individuals variously in law enforcement, news media, and political institutions may have compromised principles and judgments, sometimes leading to inappropriate favours or even illegal payments.<ref name=DailyBeastYates20110718>{{cite news|last=Underhill|first=William|title=U.K. Loses Faith in Police|url=http://www.thedailybeast.com/articles/2011/07/18/john-yates-resignation-u-k-loses-trust-in-police.html|accessdate=19 October 2011|newspaper=The Daily Beast|date=18 July 2011}}</ref> Expectations by Met officers of later employment by news organisations may also have compromised relationships. This entanglement of personal and commercial interests led some commentators to believe that a disincentive was created for police officials to thoroughly investigate allegations of wrongdoing.  This may have resulted in the failure to notify victims in a timely manner, led to misleading statements to the public and government oversight bodies to cover-up wrongdoing, and/or led to attempts to stifle the voices of whistle-blowers.

The Met also came under criticism for ignoring enormous amounts of evidence and for anaemic investigations until public disclosure of it forced them to do so.

===Performance of News International===
Initial investigations by [[News International]] had limited objectives and [[News International phone hacking scandal reference lists#Investigations|involved pre-screened evidence]].  Outside solicitors were used as the basis for issuing flawed reports with which to bolster the company's bogus "rogue reporter" claims with which News Corp. executives reassured Parliament.<ref name="smoking gun">{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-14099102|title=News International found 'smoking gun' e-mails in 2007|publisher=BBC News |date=12 July 2011 |accessdate=17 July 2011}}</ref> Ultimately the company acknowledged to the Leveson Inquiry that News International executives had destroyed evidence and covered up the truth.<ref>{{cite news|author1=O'Carroll, Lisa  |author2=Josh Halliday |name-list-style=amp |title=Rupert Murdoch admits NoW phone-hacking culture of cover-up|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/apr/26/murdoch-admits-phone-hacking-coverup|accessdate=24 September 2012|newspaper=The Guardian|date=26 April 2012}}</ref>

===Performance of political leadership===
Political parties apparent dependence upon endorsement by news organisations for election may have led leaders to turn a blind eye to how newspapers acquired their information.  [[Andy Coulson]] was editor of ''[[News of the World]]'' when [[Clive Goodman]] was convicted of hacking Royal household mobile phones.  Shortly after he resigned, maintaining he know nothing of wrongdoing but accepting responsibility for what happened on his watch, he was hired by the Conservative Party as their director of communications and later became Prime Minister David Cameron's highest paid advisor.<ref>{{cite news|author1=Quinn, Ben  |author2=James Robinson
 |name-list-style=amp |title=Andy Coulson: from Essex council house to David Cameron's inner circle|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2011/jan/21/andy-coulson-profile-resignation|accessdate=24 September 2012|newspaper=The Guardian|date=21 Jan 201}}</ref> Judgments regarding Rupert and James Murdoch's character by a Parliamentary Committee were made along party lines.<ref name="Sabbagh"/>

===Media coverage of the scandal===
With the behaviour of news media organisations at the centre of the scandal, questions were raised as to whether media coverage was stifled by ownership interests.  Initial reaction by ''The Wall Street Journal'', owned by News Corp, was to serve as a platform for owner Rupert Murdoch's response.  A commentator at Fox, also owned by News Corp, said "I'm not going to touch it."  Other industry commentators noted that the amount, aggressiveness, and focus of early media coverage of the scandal by news organisations varied widely, possibly reflecting the tension between journalistic integrity and the vested interests of the ultimate owners of those organisations.<ref name=CNN20110715>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/blogpost/post/fox-news-program-avoids-talk-of-murdochs-news-international-hacking-scandal/2011/07/15/gIQA1rV6FI_blog.html |title=Fox News, CNN confront coverage issues on Murdoch's News International hacking scandal |author=Flock, Elizabeth |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=15 July 2011 |accessdate=9 July 2011}}</ref>

The scandal generated broad interest worldwide shortly after ''[[The Guardian]]'' reported in July 2011 that murdered teenager Milly Dower's phone had been hacked into by agents of ''[[News of the World]]''<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2011/jul/04/milly-dowler-voicemail-hacked-news-of-world |title=Missing Milly Dowler's voicemail was hacked by News of the World |work=The Guardian |date=4 July 2011 |accessdate=9 August 2011 }}</ref> and after Rupert Murdoch announced that the 168-year-old newspaper would be closed as a consequence.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.sky.com/home/article/16026231 |title=NOTW Closure: James Murdoch's Full Statement |publisher=Sky News |date=7 July 2011 |accessdate=9 August 2011 }}</ref> Samples of media coverage appearing immediately after ''The Guardian'' article about Milly Dowler's phone are included with the [[phone hacking scandal reference lists]].

===Self-regulation of the press===
The [[Press Complaints Commission|UK Press Complaints Commission (PCC)]] failed to question any journalists or editorial executives after [[Clive Goodman]] was convicted, choosing to accept [[Andy Coulson]]'s assertion that the hacking was "aberrational, "a rogue exception," done by a single journalist.  [[phone hacking scandal reference lists#Investigations|Its investigation of phone hacking]] concluded there was no evidence of phone hacking beyond what had already been reported.  This report and its conclusions were ultimately withdrawn.<ref name=GuardianVerdicts20100224/><ref name="Press Complaints Commission"/>

===Public interest defence===
Some attempts were made to justify illegal acquisition of confidential information on the basis that there was a public interest in revealing dishonesty on the part of the individuals whose phones or computers were hacked.  However, distinctions were made between what was in the public interest and what was simply interesting to the public.<ref name="NYTimesMcMullan201111"/> Amelia Hill, whose journalist activity helped disclose the hacking of Milly Dowler's phone, was not prosecuted while journalists who hacked celebrities claiming it was in the public interest to reveal hypocrisy on their part, were prosecuted.

===Targeting opponents for surveillance===
During the course of various investigations into [[News International]] and their agents, the company used its own employees and hired private detectives to [[News International phone hacking scandal reference lists#Surveillance targets|conduct surveillance beyond simple phone hacking]] on a serving police officer investigating agents of ''[[News of the World]]'', two solicitors representing victims suing News International, and a member of parliament who had been critical of the company while serving on a Committee investigating it.  This surveillance reportedly included following and videotaping the target and members of his family, including young children.  It also may have included phone hacking, computer hacking, going through trash, and opening mail.

Some of this surveillance was [[News International phone hacking scandal reference lists#Solicitors|proposed by solicitors representing News International]] for the apparent purpose of discrediting individuals opposing the company.  The solicitor involved continued to characterise this surveillance as "unusual" but "justified" and "would do it again tomorrow", even after News International acknowledged that it was "deeply inappropriate".<ref name=GuardianPike20120522>{{cite news|last=O'Carroll|first=Lisa|title=Surveillance of phone-hacking victims' solicitors was justified, says lawyer|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2012/may/22/surveillance-phone-hacking-lawyers|newspaper=The Guardian|date=22 May 2012|accessdate=20 July 2012}}</ref>
